entries.title: Man, 16-year-old girl shot inside Gresham home
entries.summary: <p>A man and a 16-year-old girl were shot while inside a home in Gresham on Friday evening, Chicago police said.</p><p>Shortly before 7 p.m., a man, 49, was involved in a verbal altercation with someone he knew and was shot multiple times inside a home in the 7900 block of South Hermitage Avenue, police said.</p><p>The wounded man was transported to Advocate Christ Medical Center in critical condition, police said. A 16-year-old girl, also in the home, was struck by gunfire and taken to the same hospital in good condition.</p><p>A person of interest was questioned by police. Area detectives are investigating.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Lake View’s Kaleb Lovett owning the show in only his fourth year of football
entries.summary: <p>Kaleb Lovett didn’t play organized sports until his eighth-grade year and didn’t start tackle football until he got to high school.</p><p>Call the Lake View senior running back a fast learner.</p><p>Through the first six weeks of this season, Lovett ranked first in Illinois and 15th nationally with 1,153 rushing yards, according to the MaxPreps database. Even factoring in that not every school reports its stats, it’s a remarkable achievement for a player so new to the game.</p><p>And Lovett could be moving farther up the leaderboard after running 25 times for 296 yards and two touchdowns in the Wildcats’ epic 36-34 win over Von Steuben in five overtimes Thursday night.</p><p>How has Lovett done it? Credit his effort and an offensive line that returned all but one starter.</p><p>“I had to outwork everyone,” Lovett told the Sun-Times. “I had to do more than the regular load that everyone was taking on.”</p><p>He did, Lake View coach Kipp Duplechine confirmed.</p><p>“Coming from Louisiana, where I come from, there’s a lot of guys who run [4.4 or 4.5 in the 40-yard dash],” Duplechine said. “But work ethic-wise, he’s probably one of the top guys I’ve coached in a while. We had a banquet before the season, and I told everyone he’s the most improved player I’ve ever coached.</p><p>“Pound for pound, he’s one of the strongest guys. He only weighs like 165, but he squats with the linemen.”</p><p>Those linemen share a strong bond with Lovett, a 6-footer.</p><p>“I think the amount of appreciation he shows for us up front gives us a lot of motivation to block for him,” senior center Stephan Chi said.</p><p>Senior tackle Marc Schmidt saw Lovett’s breakout coming.</p><p>“Oh, yeah, I knew it from the start, from JV days when we were playing with each other and he would be running the ball or [playing] receiver,” Schmidt said. “He always made a statement for himself.”</p><p>Lovett didn’t get many carries last season because the Wildcats had senior Tyrone Townes, who earned All-City honorable mention and had a 300-yard rushing game against Public League North champ Curie. Lovett played mostly cornerback last year and is still doing that this season, along with a little wide receiver.</p><p>“He kind of reminds me of [Townes],” senior tackle Brent McMillin said. “His explosiveness is what really sticks out about him.”</p><p>Duplechine is reminded of former Saints quarterback and tight end Taysom Hill.</p><p>“[Lovett] was kind of like a Taysom Hill — plug him in at X, plug him in at receiver, cornerback, special teams,” he said. “But this year he just kind of locked in at tailback.”</p><p>Although Lake View is 6-1 and atop the White North at 4-0, attention isn’t always easy to come by for the Wildcats in general, or Lovett in particular. But Duplechine will be working his connections when the season is over to find a college home for his star.</p><p>“No one’s reached out yet, but it’s still very early,” Duplechine said. “We’re kind of overshadowed by Kenwood and Mount Carmel and all these other teams. But if you’re ranked No. 1 in the state in rushing and No. 15 in the country, someone’s going to call.</p><p>“He definitely has potential to play [NCAA Division 3 or 2], but I want to try to get him to a D1 school, at least an FCS school.”</p>

entries.title: Northwestern debuts Ryan Field, the most expensive college stadium ever
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >Northwestern’</a>s bold claim to the future of their sport — the most expensive college football stadium ever built — was baptized by the sounds of AC/DC’s “Thunderstruck” on Friday night.</p><p>As the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/10/01/limited-edition-willie-the-wildcat-bobblehead-commemorates-northwesterns-new-ryan-field" target="_blank" >Wildcats</a> prepared to run onto the field seconds before kickoff, the guitar licks bounced off the new concrete, old limestone and soccer-style canopy of the stadium. Players sprinted across the field and stopped in front of their new student section, the Wildcat Wall. Two thousand students stomped and kicked up an ear-splitting, Advil-reaching frenzy.</p><p>It was all so, well, not Northwestern. The Big Ten’s smallest, most demure fan base had never seen — or heard — anything like this. Moments after the Wildcats took the field, an NFL scout commented to no one in particular that it didn’t feel like a pro football stadium — it felt like an NBA arena, complete with throbbing music and flashy video.</p><p>Whether Northwestern can use the $875 million Ryan Field to its advantage remains to be seen. There were empty purple seats scattered throughout the 35,000-seat stadium — and many more covered by Penn State fans wearing white. Booster Pat Ryan’s dream stadium is unique to the Big Ten — it’s the smallest in the football-crazy league — if not the sport.</p><p>It was ready Friday because it had to be. When I took my dog for a walk eight hours before kickoff — I live down the street — employees were still screwing in streetlights and testing turnstiles with QR codes. Freshly planted flowers were being watered.</p><p>When it was clear the stadium wouldn’t be ready for the start of this season, serendipity brought Northwestern a worthy story line.</p><p>One hundred years ago to the day Friday, 18,000 fans watched the Purple beat South Dakota, 34-0, when they debuted their as-yet-unnamed $2 million stadium. Vic Gustafson scored a touchdown and then on the next play intercepted a pass and returned it for a touchdown as the first-half gun — back when they used one— sounded. Gustafson, who would go on to captain the Wildcats’ first Big Ten championship team the next year, had shared the backfield at Wheaton High School with none other than Red Grange.</p><p>A month later, the stadium was named after William Dyche, the former Evanston mayor and Northwestern vice president who had originally ordered the construction of wooden football bleachers in 1905. The Bears played there in 1970 when the NFL ruled that Wrigley Field was too small. A five-year contract to stay there was challenged by locals and eventually denied by the Big Ten. The team moved to Soldier Field the next year.</p><p>In 1997, the stadium was christened Ryan Field after the booster and longtime Northwestern Board of Trustees chair — who is the founder of AON and part-owner of the Bears — paid for a massive renovation. The stadium still felt old. In the 2008 Ernie Davis biopic “The Express,” it served as a stand-in for Syracuse’s Archbold Stadium, which had closed 30 years earlier.</p><p>The old stadium was torn down in February 2024. The Wildcats spent the interim two-and-a-half years splitting time between Martin Stadium on campus and Wrigley Field. The former, a soccer and lacrosse field steps from Lake Michigan, was fitted with expanded bleachers and food trucks. Playing at Wrigley Field in November allowed the Wildcats to avoid nastiest weather of the football season.</p><p>Construction at Central Street was met with consternation by some Evanston locals. It took a tiebreaking vote by Mayor Daniel Biss to approve the stadium plan, which included rezoning for concerts. In exchange, Northwestern agreed to contribute to various city funds and causes.Friday night, years of construction and a century of prelude produced Northwestern’s bold statement to the rest of the league.</p><p>Thunderstruck, indeed.<br></p>

entries.title: Sox postseason run has instilled pride in the South Side
entries.summary: <p>Sometimes baseball has no idea of the power it can wield. How it can ofttimes, depending on the circumstances that surround it, transcend a loss or a win, even one 21 years in the making.</p><p>“Sport has the power to change the world,” Nelson Mandela once said. “Sport can create hope where there was once only despair.”</p><p>Welcome to October. Welcome to the South Side, where despair has finally come to die.</p><p>Two seasons ago, the White Sox represented the bottomless and bottom-feeding “pit” of major-league baseball.</p><p>Today they come from a different place. Still the same side of town. Being in the American League Division Series, light-years ahead of anyone’s unrealistic thoughts, can do that to a community.</p><p>There’s the “know everything’s” claim that this is elation. That what skipper Will Venable likes to refer to as the “spirit of the team” belongs only to them. Thinking, possibly, that Munetaka Murakami’s champaign-soaked postgame meme-fest speaks only to the feeling of the team, short-sighting how an entire side of the third-largest city in America is drunk with him in that joy.</p><p>Not realizing what that team just accomplished exceeds way past baseball.</p><p>From inside Grandstand to outside on the street-level deck of Turtle’s. This ain’t just specific to 35th & Shields. This is how for a day — or seven — the people and patients walking about the Victory Center in Roseland can smile and how the kids in Adam Clayton Powell Jr. Paideia Academy in South Shore, until at least Wednesday night, can be infected with pride.</p><p>A feeling seeping inside Han Cha and Yunomi in the Stony Island Arts Bank to creeping outside Pressbox in Printer’s Row. In those eating dinner on a rainy Thursday in Ken’s on Western in Evergreen Park and getting an Italian beef or Nacho Supreme at the EZ Market outside O Block.</p><p>The Sox playing World Series-seeking baseball in October for the first time since they snatched the crown in 2005 to rewrite Chicago baseball history (a reminder: 11 years before the Cubs finally decided to shed their self-accepted “lovable losers” identity) is, as this newspaper put it, “what you don’t see in the box score.” Where we “understand how the Sox got here, what changed along the way and what the moment means to the people living it.”</p><p>It don’t rain in Southern California, but it rains bullets in the southern region of the Chi. Annie don’t live here because the sun never comes out tomorrow once you get south of Soldier Field and McCormick Place. Black being the Sox’ primary hex color because it goes with the funeral outfits so many of us on the South Side wear as customary uniforms based on the amount of services people believe we attend.</p><p>Antawun Carter and Jalil Sumerset are young diehard South Side residents and baseball savants who are finding ways to get tickets to the game Wednesday to be inside the Rate. Chance, Barack and Don C. searching their closets for postseason Sox pieces with tags still on them that they’ve been saving for just this moment. The Pope calling New Era for a new fitted.</p><p>It’s a hero’s journey that just happened to find baseball as its guide.</p><p>The first team in major-league history to lead every inning in a multiple-game postseason series is cute. But the depth of exactly what this is and reps remains far more profound than that. This isn’t about fans; this is about feelings. Feelings specific to an entire side of the city that has been continuously painted as those who are supposed to be numb to everything because of what our lives are supposed to be like on an everyday basis.</p><p>This win, this advance to the DS, this come-up before any type of come-up was thought to be logical, this culture Venable has created has infiltrated all blocks Commercial to Western, Lake Meadows to The Gardens, 18th and Blue Island Ave. to 119th and Cicero.</p><p>A less than 1% chance in April to make the postseason is the predicted market we walk around reminding ourselves of. Blurring the lines of the Sox with the lines of our lives. Happy to be trapped in their moment. Anything for the outside world to attach us to something different. To attach something positive inside of humanity to us.</p><p>For right now, for this momentary lapse in our perceived but hard to act like it doesn’t exist South Side societal anguish, the rain — at least in our minds — stops. The sun appears, if only for a week. The black we wear to match our Sox ’47s represents flyness, not funerals.</p><p>All championship teams have spirit. But until the Sox win one or even enter into that level of conversation, the true spirit of who they are, what they mean and how their impact resonates rests and breathes throughout the neighborhoods that have shouldered their burden for decades. Knowing the weight that 121 losses carries, knowing now what it feels like to have that weight lifted.</p><p>Like a roof that ain’t the ceiling. And the sun comes out. Tomorrow.</p>

entries.title: Brother Rice showcases its depth in Fenwick win
entries.summary: <p>Damari Thigpen had been taken off the return team earlier this season.</p><p>Brayden Parks is a four-star defensive lineman committed to Notre Dame.</p><p>Rocco Galasso began the year splitting time at quarterback with freshman Sam Holcomb before Holcomb won the starting job..</p><p>All of them flipped the script for No. 3 Brother Rice on Friday night as the Crusaders avoided a letdown after last week's rivalry win over Mount Carmel and pulled away to beat visiting Fenwick 42-21.</p><p>Thigpen ran a punt back 50 yards for a touchdown and almost did it again with a return to the Fenwick one-yard line. That set up the 310-pound Parks' second rushing TD of the game.</p><p>Galasso, meanwhile, stepped in with Holcomb sidelined by what coach Casey Quedenfeld called "a dental issue" and passed for 150 yards and a score for the Crusaders (5-2).</p><p>"We had to adjust based on our personnel with some of the injuries that we had and some of just misfortunes that we had going into this game," Quedenfeld said. "And you've just got to do the best that you can and move forward."</p><p>Thigpen returned one punt for a TD last season and has his sights set on the program career record of five.</p><p>"I've been working on it since last season but this year I haven't really been in a groove." Thigpen said.</p><p>Quedenfeld said the Crusaders changed returners this season after Thigpen had trouble fielding punts. But with the replacements out Friday, he resumed that role.</p><p>"Once we got close to the end of the regular season into the playoffs, he did a fantastic job returning punts and kicks," Quedenfeld said. "So hopefully he gets back into the groove like you just saw tonight. But in the beginning of the year, he was not doing what you saw tonight."</p><p>Neither was Parks, at least on offense. The consensus top-200 senior has teamed with five-star junior Kameron McGee to form an elite defensive line combo. They did their job on Friday, limiting Fenwick (4-3) to seven points over the first three quarters.</p><p>In the Week 6 win over Mount Carmel, Rice got McGee into the mix on offense with a key touchdown pass. On Friday, it was Parks' turn.</p><p>"It's definitely crazy that both of us get to just hop on the other side of the ball for a change," Parks said. "It just adds a dynamic or versatility to our offense."</p><p>Parks' first touchdown was part of a 28-0 run that turned a 7-3 first-quarter deficit into a 31-7 fourth-quarter lead.</p><p>"It's amazing, them trusting me with the ball, trusting me to punch it in," he said.</p><p>"We've been working on some different things to get guys involved," Quedenfeld said. "Whether it's Jack [McNamara] on the touchdown catch or Kameron catching the ball or different types of running backs and things like that."</p><p>McNamara's TD came on a short jump pass by Galasso, who was 13 of 22 passing with no interceptions. Jameson Davis added 118 rushing yards and a TD on 22 carries.</p><p>"Hopefully next week everyone's at full strength. whether it's running back, receiver, kick returner, punt returner, quarterback," Quedenfeld said.</p><p>Fenwick quarterback Myles Hill was 10 of 22 passing for 110 yards and one TD to Jake Thies. Hill and Thies, who had seven carries for 60 yards, also ran for touchdowns.<br></p>

entries.title: Mount Carmel QB Brady Cloherty ties his own school record with 7 TD passes against Providence
entries.summary: <p>Mount Carmel, the area’s heavily hyped, much-loved and hated football powerhouse, took its two losses on the chin this season in stoic fashion.</p><p>The Caravan didn’t make excuses, even though excuses were easily within grasp. Many fans might not even know how legitimate the excuses are.</p><p>Mount Carmel lost its starting quarterback, Ryder Startz, in the first half of the first game of the season. Then, a week later, defensive back Cullen Winters went down with an injury. Winters, a senior returning starter, was essentially the team's defensive play caller.</p><p>Senior Brady Cloherty stepped in for Startz and was immediately effective. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/10/01/high-school-football-scores-week-7" >Friday</a> against Providence, he took another step forward, throwing for 376 yards and seven touchdowns in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-football-rankings/2026/09/27/high-school-football-rankings-chicago-illinois-sun-times-michael-obrien" >No. 4 Caravan’s</a> 49-14 win against the No. 19 Celtics.</p><p>Mount Carmel's defense wasn’t as quick to adjust to missing a key player. But the Caravan is figuring it out. They shut out Providence in the second half.</p><p>“It has been tough without Cullen,” Mount Carmel defensive back Tavares Harrington, a Michigan recruit, said. “He’s a big-time player. We had to make some adjustments and took those two losses. But we are back now. We are getting in a groove, and he is coming back in a week or two, so we should be straight.”</p><p>Providence quarterback Dominic Vita connected with Hunter Long for a 93-yard touchdown with 4:52 left in the second quarter to tie the game at 14. It was all Mount Carmel from then on.</p><p>“We made some great halftime adjustments,” Caravan coach Jordan Lynch said. “It is what I’ve been looking for, to come out fast in the second half.”</p><p>Mount Carmel running back Nathan Samuels left with an injury after four carries.</p><p>“Coming in, we were going to run the ball a lot,” Cloherty said. “That changed this. So we went back to our nature—air raid—and it showed.”</p><p>Cloherty was 24-for-32 with no interceptions. He threw touchdown passes to Quentin Burrell, Jamarri Thompson, Marshaun Thornton and Danny Leyden and threw three touchdown passes to tight end Ty Kennedy, a junior transfer from Crown Point, Ind.</p><p>Kennedy has consistently become more involved in the offense.</p><p>“The receivers here are some of the best athletes in the country,” Kennedy said. “They’ve been helping me out with route running and pass catching. entries.title: What to watch for in Bears-Jets game
entries.summary:
WHEN THE BEARS HAVE THE BALL

On Jan. 5, 2025, Jets safety Ashtyn Davis picked off a deep ball intended for the Dolphins’ Jaylen Waddle. It was his second of the 32-20 winon the last day of the 2024 NFL season.

The Jets haven’t intercepted a pass since — a span of 632 passes.

They went all last season — the first under head Aaron Glenn, the 15-year cornerback who then became the Lions’ defensive coordinator — without a pick. The Jets were founded in 1960; the NFL low-water mark for interceptions during that span was the 2018 49ers’ two.

Bears offensive coordinator Press Taylor heard the stat during the offseason but said he hasn’t told his quarterbacks room about it. The Bears excel in that regard, anyway — no team in the NFL has thrown fewer interceptions since the start of 2025.

The Jets signed Nahshon Wright, the NFL’s takeaways leader last year, to a one-year, $5.5 million contract to try to solve the problem. He’s been unable to crack their rotation, playing zero snaps on defense this season. The Jets’ starting cornerback group— Azareye'h Thomas , Brandon Stephens and slot Jarvis Brownlee — has been a pleasant surprise. The Jets have allowed 171 passing yards per game, the third-fewest in the league.

They struggled in the second half last week, giving up three touchdowns points on the last four non-kneeling drives to the Lions. That matched their total in Weeks 1 and 2 — a win against the woeful Titans and a loss to the struggling Packers.

WHEN THE JETS HAVE THE BALL

The Bears consider last year’s Week 4 game — a win in Las Vegas punctuated by Josh Blackwell’s blocked field goal — a turning point in their season. Geno Smith, then, had a hand in setting the Bears toward the NFC North title.

Smith threw three interceptions to the Bears — two to Kevin Byard and one to Tyrique Stevenson — as part of a stretch of nine picks in the first five games. He finished with a league-high 17.

After returning to the team that drafted him, Smith has yet to throw an interception in three games. He’s been remarkably efficient under new offensive coordinator Frank Reich, posting a 110 passer rating that ranks fourth among quarterbacks who have thrown at least 50 passes.

It’s unclear whether Stevenson will get a chance to pick him off again. He was limited to four defensive snaps last week after pulling his hamstring against the Vikings. Rookie Malik Muhammad shined in his place, giving up three catches for 45 yards on five targets. Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen will continue to mix-and-match his personnel. Six defensive backs played at least 20% of the Bears’ snaps last week as Allen leaned on exotic dime package looks on third downs. The Bears took the ball away three times. Their six on the season ranks third in the NFL.

The Jets will be without two starters, running back Breece Hall, who will be replaced by Braelon Allen, and receiver Adonai Mitchell.

entries.title: Housing counseling services are a public investment — not favors
entries.summary: <p>For thousands of families across America, the difference between keeping a home and losing one often comes down to a single conversation.</p><p>A housing counselor can help a homeowner avoid foreclosure after a job loss, help a first-time buyer learn how to navigate the mortgage process without falling prey to predatory terms and help a renter facing eviction discover options that keep a family from becoming homeless.</p><p>These services are not political; they are practical. In many cases, they are a lifeline.</p><p>The Trump administration wants to sever that lifeline by withholding more than $56 million in congressionally approved housing counseling funds. The National Urban League and nine other nonprofit organizations have gone to federal court to challenge the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's order.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-170000" name="module-170000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Last week, a federal judge recognized the gravity of the situation. Rather than allow the funding to disappear at the end of the fiscal year while the case is litigated, U.S. District Judge Jia Cobb <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/10/01/housing-action-illinois-sues-hud-trump-administration-nonprofit-radical-left-ngo" >ordered</a> that the Sept. 30 deadline be suspended, preserving the funds until the court can decide whether the administration's actions were lawful. The court held that allowing the funding to lapse could deprive plaintiffs of any meaningful relief and maintained the status quo while the legal challenge proceeds.</p><p>The decision is not a final victory. But it was an important acknowledgment that the stakes are too high to permit the Trump administration to snatch away these resources before the courts have an opportunity to review its conduct.</p><p>Congress created the Comprehensive Housing Counseling program to help Americans seek, finance, maintain, rent and own homes and to assist homeowners facing foreclosure or homelessness. For decades, organizations across the nation have relied on these funds to provide trusted, community-based guidance for families making some of the most consequential financial decisions of their lives. The administration's proposed rescission would eliminate nearly all of the funding Congress appropriated for the program.</p><p>At a time when housing affordability has become one of the defining economic challenges of our era, that makes no sense.</p><p>In Chicago, families feel the pressure every day. Rent consumes ever-larger shares of household income. Homeownership remains out of reach for too many working families. Black families continue to face persistent racial gaps in wealth and homeownership that are the direct result of generations of discriminatory policies. Across the country, Americans are struggling with rising costs, higher borrowing expenses, and financial uncertainty.</p><p>We need more housing counseling, not less.</p><p>Yet the administration has sought to justify these cuts by portraying grant recipients as ideological adversaries rather than community service providers. According to our lawsuit, White House officials publicly described housing counseling grantees as organizations with "DEI-centric discriminatory agendas" and used related rhetoric to support the proposed funding rescission. Our complaint argues that the government targeted recipients based on viewpoints and speech protected by the First Amendment.</p><p>The Constitution does not permit presidents to punish organizations because they disagree with their views. Nor does it allow the executive branch to withhold funding that Congress lawfully appropriated simply because political leaders find certain recipients inconvenient or disagreeable.</p><p>This case is about a fundamental constitutional principle as much as it is about housing.</p><p>Congress controls federal spending. The First Amendment protects free expression. Neither protection disappears when an administration encounters criticism.</p><p>When government officials begin deciding which organizations deserve funding based on whether they are politically agreeable, they are not merely threatening individual nonprofits. They are threatening the independence of civil society itself.</p><p>The National Urban League's interest in this case is straightforward. We work every day to expand economic opportunity and help families achieve financial stability. Housing remains one of the most important pathways to wealth creation in America. For many families, homeownership is the principal asset transferred from one generation to the next. It is a foundation for educational attainment, neighborhood stability and economic security.</p><p>Housing counseling helps make that pathway possible.</p><p>A first-time homebuyer who receives sound guidance is more likely to make informed financial decisions. A homeowner struggling through temporary hardship may avoid foreclosure and preserve years of accumulated equity. A renter facing instability may find resources that prevent displacement. These services are effective precisely because they are local, practical and rooted in trusted community institutions.</p><h3>Cautious optimism</h3><p>Stripping away those services will not lower housing costs. It will not increase affordability. It will not help families achieve the American Dream.</p><p>It will only make a difficult situation worse.</p><p>The court's order gives Americans reason for cautious optimism. By preserving the funds while the legal challenge proceeds, the judge ensured that the administration cannot run out the clock and eliminate these resources before the courts assess the legality of its actions. The merits of the case remain to be decided, but the opportunity for justice remains intact.</p><p>In the months ahead, the legal arguments will unfold in court. But the broader question is: What kind of country do we want to be?</p><p>One where struggling families receive the support they need to keep a roof over their heads and pursue homeownership? Or one where access to public services depends upon political ideology and loyalty to the current holder of the Oval Office?</p><p>Housing counseling is not a political favor. It is a public investment authorized by Congress, relied upon by communities, and essential to helping families build stable futures.</p><p>The court has pressed pause. It’s up to us whether we will continue investing in opportunity, stability and the promise of homeownership for every American.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/marc-h-morial" target="_blank" ><i>Marc H. Morial</i></a><i> is president and CEO of the National Urban League</i> <i>and</i> <i>was mayor of New Orleans from 1994 to 2002.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ac0000" name="module-ac0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: Social media influencers may soon be required to disclose campaign ties
entries.summary: <p>My associate Isabel Miller and I worked on a story last week about paid influencers in campaigns. We decided to look into it after reading news reports about how the Chicago Teachers Union has been using paid influencers in its battle to control the elected Chicago school board and Mayor Brandon Johnson is also using them in his own reelection campaign.</p><p>Trouble is, the union and Johnson have not been disclosing that those influencer videos touting candidates are actually paid advertisements.</p><p>If you’re online at all, you know about these influencers. They’re usually young and some have built large followings by providing entertaining and informative content on whatever social media outlets they post on.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b30000" name="module-b30000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>For the most part, it’s legal conduct. But campaigns not disclosing influencers’ official campaign involvement appears to be illegal under current state law, which we will get to in a bit. And since the state statute doesn’t specifically mention “influencers,” some folks want to make extra special sure that they’re covered.</p><p>For example, Rep. Curtis Tarver, D-Chicago, hasn’t yet filed a bill, nor has he apparently found a vehicle bill for the upcoming fall veto session. As mentioned above, a new law might not even be strictly necessary and, whatever the case, the Legislature has not sent a single campaign reform package to the governor’s desk in years (a topic for another day). But Tarver said he plans to introduce legislation requiring social media influencers to disclose when they’re being paid to push political messages.</p><p>During an <a class="Link" href="https://wgntv.com/news/politics/wgn-the-point-politics-chicago-illinois/lawmaker-proposes-southeast-side-site-for-bears-stadium/" target="_blank" >interview</a> with WGN Political Editor Tahman Bradley late last month, Tarver said the disclosure about who or what is paying for the content could appear on screen or be spoken, and that both the campaign and the influencer should be held responsible if that disclaimer is missing.</p><p>Tarver said proposed language is with the Illinois Legislative Reference Bureau and that he hopes to move it during the fall veto session. Tarver did not respond to our questions about the proposal.</p><p>The Illinois Election Code already requires a political committee paying for communications directed at voters and mentioning a candidate to ensure its name “is identified clearly within the communication as the payor.”</p><p>State statute doesn’t mention influencers, but a political committee that pays someone to publish an online post is still responsible for ensuring the post identifies the committee as the payor, said Illinois State Board of Elections spokesperson Matt Dietrich.</p><p>“The onus is on the committee to include attribution on the video, or social media post, etc., of ‘Paid for by,’” Dietrich said. “Only the committee, not the influencer, is obligated to follow the rules of the Campaign Finance Act.”</p><p>That’s the crucial gap that Tarver wants to close.</p><p>“The campaign knows they’re paying the influencer for the purpose of influencing individuals, and the influencer knows they’re being paid to do so,” Tarver said during the WGN segment. “The campaign may disclose on a quarterly basis, or something along those lines, or weekly whereas the influencer is in real time. So both of them should be obligated to do so.”</p><p>Currently, those payments must also be disclosed on the committee’s quarterly campaign finance report. The election code requires committees to list the “full name and mailing address” of anyone paid more than $150 in aggregate during the reporting period, along with the amount, date and purpose of the expenditure.</p><p>If a campaign uses a consultant to recruit and pay influencers, the report can’t always stop at the consultant. Once payments to the consultant reach $3,000 during the quarterly reporting period, existing state statute requires the committee to disclose how much went to each influencer, why they were paid and who benefited if the consultant was “only a conduit for payment to another.”</p><p>California and Texas already have requirements aimed specifically at paid political influencers.</p><p>California requires influencers to disclose when a political committee pays for a post. A new law signed this month will make the influencer and the committee jointly liable for civil or administrative penalties if the disclosure is missing. Texas requires social media users paid to post or repost political advertising to identify who paid for it.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bc0000" name="module-bc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: How we photographed President Trump's first second-term visit to Illinois
entries.summary: <p>This week’s top photo comes from Visual Journalist <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/candace-chambers" target="_blank" >Candace Dane Chambers</a>.</p><h3><b>What makes this photo important?</b></h3><p>On Sunday, President Donald Trump made his first visit to Illinois since his reelection, serving as the honorary chairman of the Presidents Cup golf tournament. He was met with a mixed reception. Tournament attendees were largely thrilled by his appearance, while protesters outside the country club gates decried his administration’s policies. Trump gave brief remarks at the start of the day’s matches, setting the stage for a team U.S. victory over their international opponents by saying, “Our country is doing great, better than ever before.” His appearance came as polling numbers for the midterm elections point to possible trouble for the Republican Party.</p><h3><b>How I got this photo:</b></h3><p>Security was tight when Trump arrived at Medinah Country Club. Members of the media had to navigate through several checkpoints to get onto the green for the final trophy ceremony. When we were let in, we were separated into two groups — national media and PGA staff were in one central spot in front of the podium and local news organizations were relegated to a space off to the side, partially obscured by TV cameras. It was a mad dash to find an ideal vantage point, and I managed to get a seated spot on the front line, just to the right of the cameras. Golden hour was just beginning so the light worked in our favor. The trophy presentation was relatively short and well choreographed, so I just waited for the money shot of Trump handing the cup to team U.S. and continued shooting after the moment to try to get some organic reactions like the ones in this shot.</p><h3><b>Technical details:</b></h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" entries.title: Columbus Day, lynchings and Frederick Douglass' Chicago-based denunciation against racial injustice
entries.summary: <p>This month we mark Columbus Day. The first one was a Chicago story. In the fall of 1892, the nation celebrated 400 years since Columbus reached the Americas. Chicago was its grandest stage. The city dedicated the grounds of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2025/06/25/griffin-msi-online-collection-visitors-1893-worlds-fair" >World’s Columbian Exposition</a>.</p><p>When the world arrived the next spring, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/2/18/22284686/frederick-douglass-chicago-worlds-fair" >Frederick Douglass</a> was there. He was the most photographed American of his century. At 75, he ran the Haitian Pavilion for the government of Haiti. Ida B. Wells worked beside him, putting a pamphlet into the hands of foreign visitors. She sent out 10,000 copies. When hecklers jeered one of his speeches, Douglass threw aside his notes and spoke right over them.</p><p>The pamphlet asked why African Americans had been left out of the fair's exhibits and planning. Douglass had a place at the exposition only because Haiti gave him one. He wrote the pamphlet's opening as a wish list. Every item on it was something he could not honestly tell the world.</p><p>He wished he could say the national government "is not a rope of sand." A rope of sand looks strong. It holds nothing. Douglass meant a government too weak to protect "American citizens of whatever color, at home." He wished he could say it would send warships to punish "the murder of its citizens in New Orleans." Washington sent warships when Americans were harmed overseas. Douglass knew. He had been America's top diplomat in Haiti. At home, the government did nothing.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-050000" name="module-050000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Everyone who received their message knew what had happened in New Orleans. Two years earlier, the city saw one of the <a class="Link" href="https://www.history.com/articles/the-grisly-story-of-americas-largest-lynching" target="_blank" >largest mass lynchings</a> in American history. The victims were Italians and Italian Americans.</p><p>On March 14, 1891, a lynch mob broke into the jail. It killed 11 men accused in the murder of the city's police chief. Three had just been found not guilty. Three had a trial end with no verdict. Five had never been tried. No one was ever punished for their murders.</p><p>Italy's top diplomat in Washington said only three or four of the dead were Italian citizens. The rest were Americans, or on their way to becoming Americans. Italy wanted the killers tried. It wanted payment for the victims' families. Secretary of State James G. Blaine said Washington could not promise a trial. Murder was Louisiana's business. Italy called its diplomat home.</p><p>President Benjamin Harrison admitted the problem to Congress. He asked Congress to let federal courts try crimes against foreigners. Congress did nothing.</p><p>So the government paid instead. In April 1892, the United States gave Italy 125,000 francs, about $25,000, for the victims' families. Blaine wrote that the president hoped the money would "efface all memory of the unhappy tragedy." In other words, forget it. Italy said the two nations were friends again.</p><p>Three months later, Harrison proclaimed a national holiday for Columbus. That fall, Washington sent two warships to Genoa for Italy's own Columbus celebration.</p><p>The same government that could not protect 11 men in a New Orleans jail sent warships to honor Italy. The first Columbus Day was declared in the shadow of the lynching.</p><p>Italy had a king and a navy. The families of its citizens got paid. The families of the Italian Americans killed beside them got nothing.</p><h3>Lynching of Black Americans brushed off </h3><p>When a lynch mob turned on these European immigrants, smeared as criminals, the world took notice. African Americans lived with that danger every day. In 1891 alone, the Chicago Tribune counted 169 African Americans killed by lynch mobs. Their families got nothing. No foreign power spoke for them. No warship sailed.</p><p>Congress waited 131 years to make lynching a federal crime. The <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/117th-congress/house-bill/55" target="_blank" >Emmett Till Antilynching Act</a> became law in 2022. Until then, the rope was sand.</p><p>The first Columbus Day asked Americans to look away from a lynch mob and toward a hero. In one sense, it worked. Italian Americans are safe today in ways their great-grandparents were not.</p><p>But the terror did not end. It moved. In time, the Ku Klux Klan would come for Catholic immigrants of every kind. For African Americans, the danger changed shape. It did not end. Too often, the killers had friends in government.</p><p>Douglass refused to let the world look away. He said what the government would not. Black Americans were being "tortured, shot, hanged or burned to death," he wrote. They died "without ever seeing a judge, a jury or advocate." In the same breath, he named New Orleans, reminding all that Black Americans were not the only ones whose rights and lives were put at risk by a weak federal response to lynch mobs.</p><p>He also held out something better. Douglass asked whether America was "the better or the worse" for being made of many peoples. His answer was better. Every nation has a mission, he said, rooted in its "character and composition." America's was plain. It was to become the most perfect "national illustration of the unity and dignity of the human family that the world has ever seen."</p><p>That is still our mission. This Columbus Day, let us remember the context of the first one. And let us reflect on how far we have come, or not, since then.</p><p><i>Ben Jealous is a professor of practice at the University of Pennsylvania and former president and CEO of the NAACP.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c60000" name="module-c60000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Lawmakers look to require AM radio in new cars despite automakers' pushback
entries.summary: <p>A bipartisan effort to require AM radio in new vehicles is advancing in Congress, setting up what supporters say could be a major win for broadcasters and the medium.</p><p>Last month, the U.S. House passed the AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act that would require automakers to include AM radio in new vehicles at no additional cost to consumers. The bill awaits action in the Senate, where a companion measure has already garnered support, according to public records.</p><p>Broadcasters said AM radio remains a critical source of information, offering news and weather alerts, particularly when cell networks and internet service are disrupted or unreliable. And Chicago remains one of the country's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2023/6/5/23750177/chicago-am-radio-electric-vehicles-buzzkill" >most influential radio markets</a>, with several well-known AM stations attracting listeners for news, sports and talk programming.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure era.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times archives</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“AM radio — all radio — has always been about connection, and in Chicago, especially, the connection is incredibly strong,” Mary Sandberg Boyle, vice president and general manager of WGN-AM 720, said. “You don't need a subscription. You don't need a data plan or an app. You turn on the radio, and it's there.”</p><p>Chicago is the third-largest radio market in the country, with an estimated listener population of roughly 8 million, according to Nielsen Audio market rankings.</p><p>Boyle said the accessibility of radio becomes especially important during severe weather and breaking news situations.</p><p>“That's when local radio is really more important because we have the ability to stay live, pivot our content and what we're covering, and we can access a large amount of audience members very quickly and keep everybody safe,” she said.</p><p>Boyle also serves on the board of directors of the National Association of Broadcasters, which has argued that preserving AM radio access is an access issue rather than a matter of nostalgia.</p><p>The legislation emerged after several automakers removed AM radio from certain electric vehicle models, citing interference from electric power systems. Companies including Tesla, Rivian, Volvo and others have either eliminated or limited AM radio in some EVs.</p><p>The Alliance for Automotive Innovation, which represents most major automakers, has opposed the requirement. In congressional testimony last year, President and CEO John Bozzella argued that "analog AM radio does not contribute to motor vehicle safety" and requiring it as standard equipment "is not necessary to ensure public safety."</p><p>Under the bill, the U.S. Department of Transportation would be required to develop regulations ensuring AM radio remains available in new vehicles sold in the U.S. The measure would also bar automakers from charging consumers separately for AM radio access.</p><p>Senate leaders haven’t announced when the measure could receive a floor vote.</p><h3>Evolving media landscape</h3><p>While public discussion around the legislation has largely focused on emergency alerts and news access, some scholars say preserving AM radio also has implications for media diversity.</p><p>“AM radio is fascinating,” Zachary McDowell, associate professor of communications at the University of Illinois Chicago, said. “It allows for a lot more diversity in content.”</p><p>He said many immigrant and language-focused stations operate on the AM band, providing programming that may not be widely available elsewhere.</p><p>“I think the media landscape is really overwhelmingly homogenized right now, and AM radio is important in many markets,” he said. “It's a space that still allows for all sorts of different voices that is still open and accessible.”</p><p>The format has remained popular because listeners can’t find similar programming anywhere else, said Rodney Gibbs, executive director of Heartland Signal, which operates progressive talk radio station WCPT-AM 820.</p><p>"Despite the kind of shiny objects that digital media is, AM radio still has a viable and durable audience," Gibbs said. "It's a daily, unscripted, authentic conversation between the host and the listeners. You don't get that from broadcast television. You don't get that from digital media."</p><p>Gibbs also said station operators increasingly see the medium as part of a broader media ecosystem.</p><p>"AM radio remains the heart of what we do," he said. "But it's the beginning. It's not the end."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2023/6/5/23750177/chicago-am-radio-electric-vehicles-buzzkill" >Chicago’s a big market for AM radio, but electric vehicles loom as a buzzkill</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Take caution, but don't avoid fruits, vegetables during contamination outbreaks
entries.summary: <p>Back-to-school season changes the rhythm of Chicago kitchens. Mornings get earlier, lunchboxes return to the counter, and families once again need food that is quick, nourishing and appealing enough that children will actually eat it.</p><p>This year, food safety headlines have added uncertainty. Some families are asking whether they should stop buying fresh produce. The concern is understandable, and every outbreak deserves a serious response. But abandoning fruits and vegetables is not what health officials are advising.</p><p>A July<a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/cyclospora-outbreak-fda-opinion-poll/" target="_blank" > CBS News/YouGov poll</a> found that 4 in 10 Americans were buying or eating less produce because of the recent cyclospora outbreak. That worries me. Many families already struggle to eat enough fruits and vegetables. A necessary precaution should not become fear of an entire grocery aisle.</p><p>The better response is informed confidence. When health officials identify a concern, follow their specific guidance rather than assuming it applies to every fruit and vegetable. Check current U.S. <a class="Link" href="https://www.fda.gov/food/outbreaks-foodborne-illness/investigation-multistate-outbreak-cyclospora-illnesses-iceberg-lettuce-july-2026?utm_source" target="_blank" >Food and Drug Administration</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.cdc.gov/cyclosporiasis/outbreaks/07-26/investigation.html?utm_source" target="_blank" >Centers for Disease Control and Prevention</a> advisories. At home, stick with <a class="Link" href="https://www.fda.gov/food/buy-store-serve-safe-food/selecting-and-serving-produce-safely" target="_blank" ><u>habits that protect families every day</u></a>: Wash hands and preparation surfaces, keep produce separate from raw meat and seafood, rinse fruits and vegetables under running water and refrigerate perishable items promptly.</p><p>Then bring the joy back. Add vegetables to a familiar family meal or tuck fruit into a lunchbox. Fresh, frozen and canned choices can all help families build nourishing meals within their budgets and traditions.</p><p>Strawberries are an example I especially love. They fit easily into busy days — sliced over oatmeal, blended into a smoothie or simply rinsed and eaten. I have visited California strawberry farms and seen firsthand the <a class="Link" href="https://www.californiastrawberries.com/strawberries-safe-to-eat/" target="_blank" ><u>care growers put into the fruit they bring to market and to their own families.</u></a></p><p>Food producers and regulators carry the primary responsibility for prevention, rapid detection and clear communication. Consumers should not have to decode vague warnings.</p><p>As a dietitian, I do not ask families to choose between food safety and good nutrition. We need both. Follow reliable guidance, practice sensible food handling and keep nourishing foods on the table. Caution belongs in the produce aisle. So do confidence, appetite and joy.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.hispanicnutrition.com/who-we-are/" target="_blank" ><i>Sylvia Meléndez Klinger</i></a><i>, dietitian, founder, Hispanic & Multicultural Nutrition Communications, and 2025 recipient, Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics Medallion Award</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d90000" name="module-d90000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Amtrak rail yard belongs on industrial site</h3><p>Picture a massive diesel fuel tank in your backyard. Now surround it with a 24-hour railroad maintenance facility: locomotives, fueling, lights, trucks, noise and emissions.</p><p>That is what<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/09/17/chinatown-and-bridgeport-residents-press-amtrak-leaders-to-pump-the-breaks-on-rail-yard-plan" > Amtrak</a> wants to put beside thousands of South Side residents.</p><p>Amtrak already has a maintenance facility. It sits on 47 acres along the Chicago River in a largely industrial corridor. According to figures cited by 11th Ward Ald. Nicole Lee, just <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/news/public-meeting-thursday-amtrak-white-sox-stadium-plans/" target="_blank" >26 people</a> live within 500 feet of the existing facility. More than 6,000 live within 500 feet of the proposed Canal Street site.</p><p>Amtrak says it needs a new, modern facility. Fine. But that doesn’t explain why it needs to be here.</p><p>The land beneath Amtrak’s existing facility has become extremely valuable. Billionaire investor and White Sox minority owner Justin Ishbia has that property under contract, while his Canal Edge LLC is developing and delivering Amtrak’s replacement facility.</p><p>The result is difficult to ignore: A 24-hour industrial operation is being moved away from a place where almost nobody lives and into a densely populated area.</p><p>Amtrak also points to the 3,000 union jobs it says construction will support. Bridgeport is a pro-union community. But those jobs aren’t tied to South Canal and 33rd streets. Union workers can build or modernize a facility at an appropriate industrial location.</p><p>And location matters. In 2019, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/1/6/18413174/diesel-fuel-spill-in-south-loop-train-yard-prompts-hazmat-response" >2,800 gallons of diesel </a>spilled at Amtrak’s existing Chicago facility. Industrial facilities have accidents. That’s one reason we put them in industrial areas rather than beside homes, schools, parks and playgrounds.</p><p>Chicago is a railroad city with extensive rail infrastructure and industrial land. If Amtrak cannot modernize its existing yard, find a genuinely nonresidential alternative.</p><p>This isn’t an argument against Amtrak, modernization or union jobs. It’s an argument against putting a massive 24-hour industrial operation beside thousands of people when we already know it doesn’t have to be.</p><p>Stop this project. Find another site.</p><p><i>Kathleen M. Hughes, Bridgeport</i></p><h3>Sen. Duckworth, hold Trump and his cronies accountable</h3><p>For 20 months, the Trump administration has relentlessly attacked our democracy and civil liberties. Chicago, in particular, has reeled under the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/07/09/ice-arrests-increase-chicago-tactics-less-publicized-midway-blitz-back-yards-gage-brighton-park" >deployment of federal paramilitary</a> forces intended to terrorize residents and <a class="Link" href="https://wgntv.com/news/chicago-news/i-wonder-about-their-intentions-chicago-pastor-speaks-out-after-ice-agents-shoot-him-in-head-with-pepper-balls-in-broadview/" target="_blank" >chill</a> freedoms of speech and assembly. But for some reason Sen. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., recently <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/reel/DdpuO_ZMO--/" target="_blank" >said</a> if the Democrats take the House back in November all she wants to do is "move the ball forward" and allow Donald Trump a way to “save face.”</p><p>The American people don't want to help Trump save face. A majority —55% — want to see him <a class="Link" href="https://www.gelliottmorris.com/p/2026-04-22-strength-in-numbers-verasight-impeachment-polling" target="_blank" >impeached</a>, including more than 80% of Democrats. The demand for accountability has even crossed party lines. Congress <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/speaker-johnson-recesses-house-early-blocking-massies-push-to-impeach-hegseth" target="_blank" >abruptly recessed</a> last month when Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., surprised leadership with a push to <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/homenews/house/6094700-thomas-massie-house-gop-pete-hegseth-impeachment/" target="_blank" >impeach</a> Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.</p><p>Duckworth’s statement is out of line with fellow Americans, but right in line with establishment Democratic leadership. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., insists impeachment is <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/homenews/house/5849707-democrats-decline-trump-impeachment/" target="_blank" >not a priority</a>, and Jamie Raskin, D-Md., ranking member of the Judiciary Committee, says that it’s more important to <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/jamie-raskin-trump-impeachment-democrats-priorities-house-rcna596335" target="_blank" >“end the lawlessness.”</a> </p><p>The question for the Democrats is how, exactly, they plan to “move on” if they won’t impose consequences.</p><p>Does “moving on” mean that Trump gets to keep the more than <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/trumps-2b-income-in-2025-raises-fresh-questions-about-profiting-off-presidency" target="_blank" >$2 billion </a>he’s enriched himself with during his presidency? What about the white supremacist <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/interactive/2026/09/21/how-trump-turned-refugee-bureau-into-410-million-deportation-operation/" target="_blank" >Office of Remigration</a> and the approved or pledged $400 million to fund secretive "third-country" deportation agreements? Does helping Trump “save face” mean that we skip past accountability for the masked paramilitary forces who have detained people without due process? What does “moving on” look like for the families of people killed by the U.S. government in broad daylight and then lied about to the American public?</p><p>Trump and his enablers must face consequences for their abuses of power, full stop.</p><p>Duckworth is a veteran. So am I. We swore the same oath to defend the Constitution against all enemies, foreign and domestic. It is time to uphold that oath, senator. Find your courage. Demand accountability. Demand justice. Defend this democracy and call for the impeachment, conviction and removal of Trump from office.</p><p><i>Keira Havens, executive director, </i><a class="Link" href="https://citizensimpeachment.com/" target="_blank" ><i>Citizens’ Impeachment</i></a></p><h3>Single mothers hit hard by SNAP restrictions</h3><p>Ask a single mother on the West Side what she's keeping an eye on this year, and she’ll say Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, recertification: the county letter with a deadline, a list of documents and the shift she must skip to gather them.</p><p>She is reading the situation correctly. Under the 2025 federal budget law, states now cover 75% of SNAP administration costs, an increase from the previous federal-state 50% split. Illinois puts its share at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/27/illinois-sees-16-drop-in-snap-enrollment-one-year-after-food-program-overhaul" >roughly $80 million</a> a year. If the state’s SNAP error rate stays above 10%, Illinois will owe a federal penalty of <a class="Link" href="https://capitolnewsillinois.com/news/illinois-food-assistance-error-rate-continues-to-grow-as-federal-penalties-loom/" target="_blank" >$550 million to $700 million</a>. It doesn't bode well that SNAP payment error rate in Illinois was 11.56% in fiscal year 2024 — the fifth-highest in the country.</p><p>Those costs land in a city where the Greater Chicago Food Depository finds that <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagosfoodbank.org/2026-hunger-in-chicago-report/" target="_blank" >36% of households</a> lack consistent access to enough food, climbing to 47% among households with children. Statewide, 45% of SNAP benefits go to households with children.</p><p>At <a class="Link" href="https://newmoms.org/" target="_blank" >New Moms</a>, which works with young mothers across the West Side, that math is what we've talking these days. A recent Jeremiah Program and Urban Institute <a class="Link" href="https://jeremiahprogram.org/press_releases/jeremiah-program-and-urban-institute-release-national-report-on-the-needs-of-single-mothers/" target="_blank" >survey</a> of nearly 1,800 single mothers in 43 states, found matching numbers: 85% had experienced food insecurity, 97% had faced housing hardship and 64% had quit, declined or changed a job because childcare did not work.</p><p>None of that reads distant in Austin, Englewood or Little Village, where the mothers walking into our programs are doing the math.</p><p>If we can design a program for single mothers who are employed and in school with a child at home, the hardest version of the problem is solved for most others. </p><p>If you fund programs in this city, look at where your dollars land now that the state pays the bill. If you lead an organization that touches these families, come sit at the table. It is still being set.</p><p><i>Laura Zumdahl, president and CEO, New Moms</i><br><i>Chastity Lord, president and CEO,</i><a class="Link" href="https://jeremiahprogram.org/?utm_source=google&utm_medium=cpc&utm_campaign=Brand&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=20249914449&gbraid=0AAAAApU-KJJtfE07uJQB5K1gwtKOeN20e&gclid=Cj0KCQjw5vLVBhCiARIsAD56SFJsJIxGSxC3VYFJht4oPUwLZwN8J_8X7fOWJ1iPeqyUwtLH0L5UNVgaAuZLEALw_wcB" target="_blank" ><i> Jeremiah Program</i></a></p><h3>Rooting for renters rights </h3><p>Greta Connor, a "mom-and-pop landlord" in Evanston, contends in a recent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/09/30/phd-senior-citizen-landlords-cubs-sox-cta-security-trump-ad-iran-war" >letter</a> to the Sun-Times that landlords only pass on costs to renters out of necessity, not out of greed. Her tenants didn't force her to purchase two properties. Why is it her renters' responsibility to pay off the mortgages she and her husband took on voluntarily? Landlords don't become landlords out of the goodness of their hearts. They rent properties to make a profit. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/16/brandon-johnson-renters-protection-ordinance-aldermen-dueling-proposals-chicago-city-council-housing-committe" >Protecting Renters Ordinance</a> is good for tenants. Good for Mayor Brandon Johnson for standing up for us.</p><p><i>Kathryn Flucht, Boystown</i></p><h3>Rein in unlicensed drivers </h3><p>Gun control, undocumented immigrants and artificial intelligence have gotten much attention in recent years, but why aren't we targeting unlicensed drivers?</p><p>This too is a major social issue. Various national studies have found these operators running at a rate anywhere from <a class="Link" href="https://trid.trb.org/View/1156375" target="_blank" >2.7 to nine times</a> above their licensed counterparts for crashes and fatalities. Zooming in on local potential problems, I tabulated the police blotter page entries in the local neighborhood papers over the last two months. I found traffic stops outnumbering DUIs by a factor of four and above the speeders at a rate of 3 to 2. Serious stuff here, and lots of it.</p><p>Hopefully the day is coming when we'll be seeing all our cars equipped with voice or fingerprint recognition technology. If your machine consults various databases and detects a problem with your license or vehicle plates, your car will refuse to start. And if this also serves to deter a few car thieves, so much the better.</p><p>The technology for it is probably already here; it's only a question of whether and when public demand will catch up. Such a fix can't come too soon. With so many illegal motorists out there running under the radar, I think we're due to shine some more light on the trouble and lower the radar on the rogue drivers.</p><p><i>Tom Gregg, Niles </i></p><h3>Moneyball </h3><p>As a sports fan, I find the MLB playoffs unsatisfying. Not with regard to the quality of the games, but more so about the integrity of seeking competitive balance. Everyone loves a good David vs. Goliath story, but in actuality how often do the Davids win?</p><p>In this year's MLB playoffs the disparity in the participating teams payrolls is embarrassingly lopsided. The Dodgers payroll hovers around <a class="Link" href="https://sports.yahoo.com/rob-manfred-thinks-dodgers-spending-is-a-great-thing-as-payroll-hovers-around-400-million-225422948.html?guccounter=1&guce_referrer=aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuZ29vZ2xlLmNvbS8&guce_referrer_sig=AQAAAM13Z29-ixMR8ocuMxyc5cDzPb-OriNFZESRcSxyQcgf8QF0MFbdqVPgdiQ9tf7gPAE2LhG-xe1oZZMDLKgduUsp8zhxhtfLR1TobN2BUnYln-N1V5rHIGPRK2eSxblahmfu-O2BgHhNfMJJmDbL5vU7T5hoJk8T6_CbSN9kI571" target="_blank" >$400 million</a>, and the Yankees, Phillies, Braves, Padres, Astros and Cubs are all in the $250 million or more payroll club. For the remaining teams it must feel like racing against Usain Bolt and giving him a 20-yard head start. Even fans of Goliath can't feel good knowing they beat an undermanned opponent.</p><p>In the spirit of promoting fair play, I propose changing the playoff rules to require teams participating to set their rosters at a predetermined payroll dollar amount. The aim is to promote a fairer competition on the field instead of being based on bank accounts.</p><p><i>Steven Fortuna, Naperville</i><br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Family gatherings marred by hate speech
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> All members of my family are white. When my children were smaller, an incident occurred at a family holiday. One relative has a history of making racist comments, so this time we told everyone that if it happened again, we would leave. He did, and we left. My husband raised his voice at that person and made polite excuses to everyone else about leaving early. Then we all stood up from the table, packed our things and drove two hours home instead of spending the night as originally planned.</p><p>I will not repeat to you the comments that were made, but they were not microaggressions or subtle remarks. They were disgusting and violent, and I refuse to tolerate it. However, everyone else who was there disagreed with us. They said my husband ruined a perfectly nice family dinner and should apologize to keep the peace. I have told them repeatedly that they should apologize to us for making us stand up alone. They keep calling intervention-style family meetings to confront us about our behavior and say we need to repair the rift my husband caused. Were we out of line? — <i>FAMILY FRICTION</i></p><p><b>DEAR FAMILY FRICTION:</b> That dinner was far from "perfectly nice." Your husband was not out of line, and I applaud you for taking a stand. It's too easy to downplay this kind of behavior for the sake of family harmony. By acting as a willing audience, your extended family became complicit in the hate speech. Unless they promise it will never happen again, I see no reason for you to attend any future gatherings with this questionable crowd.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My siblings and I have a niece and nephew, our late sister's children, both in their 40s. The niece is grounded, level-headed, and emotionally and intellectually strong. The nephew used to be like that but now can be a lot more sensitive and overly emotional and has a somewhat controlling wife.</p><p>Our problem is that months and months, sometimes years, go by without hearing anything from them. Our nephew doesn't return phone calls in general, but if we reach out when there's a death or a hospitalization in the family, the niece processes things normally. Our nephew turns into a bowl of emotional jelly. He cries and is emotionally draining when we all need to pull together for someone else. When we explain that we can make time for him but that he needs to answer our calls or return them, he promises to do so but never follows through. His mental health is not good (and perhaps his wife isolates him), but we are at our wits' end. How do we deal with this behavior? — <i>EXASPERATED UNCLE IN OHIO</i></p><p><b>DEAR UNCLE:</b> This is the pattern your troubled nephew has established, and it isn't likely to change. Deal with his emotionally draining behavior by making sure your niece is the one who gives him the news he needs to have. If he calls you for one of those draining conversations, limit the length and do not allow him to sap you.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: What's it like to attend a phone-free concert? Here's what you told us
entries.summary: <p>We asked readers to tell us about attending concerts and other performances where they were required to be phone-free. Here's what you told us, lightly edited for clarity:</p><p>"Jill Scott, August 2026 [at The Chicago Theatre]. They put phones in a locked bag that you could hold onto."<br><i>— Tim Thomas</i></p><p>"Jack White in 2022 at UIC. It slowed down things getting in and out, but in general no phones once you were in was good. I could see it being problematic though. If my parents needed to reach us about a babysitting issue, there would have been no good way to do it."<br><i>— Arcadia Kust McCauley</i></p><p>"The Paper Machete variety show at the Green Mill every Saturday afternoon is a no video, no photo event. It is refreshing to watch the show without the distraction of a phone held up and blocking the view. The crowd is in the moment, as it should be."<br><i>— Jimmy Pobol</i></p><p>"Friday night at the Vic for Gary Clark Jr. The Yondr pouches were in use. It was fine. I miss not being able to take video of the show though."<br><i>— Chris Perez</i></p><p>"<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/09/20/review-phoebe-bridgers-the-lost-tour-united-center" >Phoebe Bridgers</a> [at the United Center]. ... It was wonderful and a good learning experience of better communication for my daughter and her friends. It was a joy to watch her express real emotions and soak in the live music she loves so much."<br><i>— Hope Zawaski</i></p><p>"Jack White at the Salt Shed on July 24. At first I was a little annoyed, but I actually enjoyed not having the device. There were plenty of professional pictures the next day to download. ... It also wasn't a hassle. Your phone fits in a little locked pouch which is quickly unlocked when you exit. It actually was a more enjoyable concert since I wasn't distracted from the real reason I was there — the music."<br><i>— Tony Scavo</i></p><p>"I would like to say Jack White in July at Radius was phone free (and it was because my phone was locked in a pouch), but it sure wasn’t phone free to get in the door. Literally the only way to get in the door was downloading an app to your phone. So shows need to make up their minds."<br><i>— Don Anderson</i><br></p>

entries.title: 'All heat-related deaths are preventable' but in the Chicago area 16 died from heat this summer
entries.summary: <p>Tanja Sopys waited for her brother, David, to arrive at her South Side home in early July.</p><p>Instead, a Chicago Transit Authority worker rang her doorbell after finding her brother’s medications left behind on a bus.</p><p>“My wife takes that, so I know how important it is,” the worker could be heard saying in her home security video.</p><div class="Enhancement"
