class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>It would be days before Tanja Sopys would learn her brother died that same day — July 1. She wasn’t notified about his death until after an autopsy was performed, determining he died from hyperthermia due to heat exposure while Chicago was under an extreme heat warning.</p><p></p><p>Tanja Sopys pieced together David's whereabouts in the days leading up to his death. He’d left the south suburban mental health rehabilitation facility where he had been living. At some point, he ended up at a Chicago hospital. When she was finally able to talk to her brother by phone, he told her he was planning to live at a different facility on the North Side, but he wouldn’t provide specifics.</p><p>He asked her for money. “I’m like, ‘Well, David, why don’t you just come here and get it,’” Tanja Sopys recalls telling her brother. “He was like, ‘I’ll come over there.’”</p><p>That was the last time she heard from him. David Sopys, 46, died 31 years after his own father died at the same age from the heat.</p><p>“He was a ‘95 heat stroke victim,” Tanja Sopys said about their father. ”So he died the same way — from the heat.”</p><p>Their father was among the hundreds in Chicago who died during <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2016/8/30/18354264/a-look-back-at-chicago-s-deadly-1995-heat-wave" >the deadly hot summer of 1995</a>. More than three decades later and following reforms — such as how the <a class="Link" href="https://www.weather.gov/lot/1995_HeatWave" target="_blank" ><u>National Weather Service</u></a> warns the public about extreme heat by issuing advisories ahead of time — hundreds no longer die from extreme heat in Chicago.</p><p>But now another Sopys is part of a spike in heat deaths in the Chicago area. More people — 16 — died from the heat in Cook County this summer than in any previous year in the last decade, according to a WBEZ and Chicago Sun-Times analysis of county data. Experts say heat-related deaths should be preventable and those who died from the heat this summer leave behind questions about what individuals and Chicago officials can do to adapt to and mitigate future stretches of extreme heat.</p><p>“Essentially all heat-related deaths are preventable,” said Kristie Ebi, professor at the Center for Health and the Global Environment at the University of Washington. “And one needs a sense of the size of the problem to provide incentives, motivations for investments in heatwave early warning and response systems, in understanding the distribution of the vulnerable groups so that one could invest appropriately into the regions that have more vulnerable people.”</p><p>Before this year, the most heat-related deaths the county had experienced in the past decade was eight, in 2022 and 2024, according to the analysis.</p><p>The Cook County Medical Examiner's Office flags some deaths as "heat related" in its online case archive, which dates back to 2015. WBEZ and the Sun-Times looked at hundreds of deaths since 2015 and identified heat-related deaths by using that flag as well as cases mentioning a primary or secondary cause of death as "heat stress," "heat stroke" or "hyperthermia." Reporters then ruled out cases not tied to warm weather.</p><p>Eleven of the 16 people who died from the heat this year either died or experienced symptoms that led to their deaths during a stretch of extreme heat and high humidity from June 29 to July 3, according to data from the Cook County medical examiner’s office. Chicago’s Office of Emergency Management and Communications issued an extreme heat warning on June 28 and then later extended the warning until July 3.</p><p>During that stretch, the city experienced four consecutive days of high temperatures ranging from 92 to 95 degrees, with temperatures falling slightly to 88 degrees by July 3.</p><p>A few of the people, like Sopys, were found outside, but others were found in homes with no working air conditioning.</p><p>On July 2, when the temperature reached 95 degrees, David Gonzalez, 44, collapsed while moving out of a Chicago Lawn home, just blocks from where David Sopys was found the day before. Otto Kendzior, 63, was found Aug. 4 inside a car that had hot air running on a day when temperatures reached 86 degrees. Joseph W. Huff, of Oak Lawn, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/30/extreme-heat-wave-death-chicago-cook-county-oak-lawn-july-stroke-stress-elderly-air-conditioning" target="_blank" ><u>who was 65 and just settling into his retirement years</u></a>, was among at least nine area residents who were found in their homes, according to records from the Cook County medical examiner’s office.</p><p>In seven of those cases, including Huff’s death, investigators noted there weren’t any working air conditioners in the homes. In Evanston, Daniel Machnikowski, 69, was found next to an air conditioning unit that had not been installed.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-a40000" name="html-embed-module-a40000"></a><div style="min-height:544px" id="datawrapper-vis-sh9t3"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/sh9t3/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-sh9t3"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/sh9t3/full.png" alt="Sixteen people have died so far this year in Cook County from heat-related causes, the most in at least a decade (Column Chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>How the body enters heat stroke</b></h3><p>During extreme heat, the human body sends blood to its edges — like the arms and legs — to keep its central organs cool, said Dr. Sheetal Khedkar Rao, co-investigator at the University of Illinois Chicago’s Center for Extreme Conditions and Health Excellence. Some of the first signs of the heat altering a person’s body will be visible through rashes and swelling of the ankles.</p><p>As the brain and heart get less blood, a person enters heat exhaustion, Rao said. A person will feel more fatigue, get headaches, experience cramps and could feel nauseous.</p><p>“This is the stage where things can go in the wrong direction if you don’t act in a way to cool down,” Rao said, adding that a person’s condition can escalate to a heat stroke unless the person can hydrate and cool down.</p><p>During a heat stroke, there's less blood flowing throughout the body because of how much the person has sweated, Rao said. At this point, a person’s brain, along with other organs like the heart, are getting very little blood. A change in a person’s mental state is associated with heat stroke and some individuals may feel confused, Rao said.</p><p>An altered mental state was noted in at least<b> </b>three<b> </b>of this year’s heat-related Cook County deaths, according to county records.</p><p>When a person is experiencing a heat stroke, their heart will beat even faster to get enough oxygen to the body but it’s doing so with less blood, Rao said. A person may not even sweat because the body has used up all of its fluids, she said. Still, their body temperature could be as hot as 104 degrees.</p><p>“They may not even complain of thirst because their brain isn’t functioning normally, it hasn’t gotten enough blood flow,” Rao said. “If they have a fever and they’re overheated and they’re confused, that is an absolute emergency.”</p><p>If a person’s body temperature is recorded, investigators use it to determine if a death was heat related, said Dr. Ponni Arunkumar, chief medical examiner at the Cook County medical examiner’s office. If the person’s body temperature is not known, that may lead to heat being recorded as a contributing factor rather than the primary cause of death, she said.</p><p>Investigators are also looking for other factors like the temperature of the place where the person was found and if there were air conditioners, Arunkumar said.</p><p>Many of those who died had recorded body temperatures that neared or exceeded 104 degrees, according to county records. David Sopys had a recorded temperature of 107 degrees when he arrived at Little Company of Mary Medical Center.</p><p>Paramedics transported Sopys to the hospital after people called 911 at about 6:30 p.m. on July 1, reporting that he had fallen near 63rd Street and Campbell Avenue in the Chicago Lawn neighborhood. He was pronounced dead two hours later.</p><p>Temperatures at Midway International Airport had reached 94 degrees that day.</p><h3><b>More vulnerable to heat injury</b></h3><p>During an autopsy, investigators look for kidney damage to determine what role heat played in the death, Arunkumar said. They also check for any substances the person may have taken prior to the death.</p><p>“Looking at all of that information, then we’ll determine whether the death is due to or related to heat,” Arunkumar said. “We are very aware that most of these deaths are preventable, so we keep our data transparent.”</p><p>Rao said patients living with chronic conditions and those living in areas with little tree canopy can be most at risk for heat-related injuries. But Rao said heat-related injuries and deaths can happen even to unsuspecting healthy individuals. She urges patients to start hydrating before a heat wave starts.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Dr. Sheetal Khedkar Rao, co-investigator at the University of Illinois Chicago’s Center for Extreme Conditions and Health Excellence.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Medications for chronic conditions can work against the person’s body navigating extreme heat, Rao said. For example, diabetics could be taking diuretic medications, commonly known as water pills, which could exacerbate how much fluids a person is losing, Rao said.</p><p>Heart patients on medications known as beta blockers, which slow the heart down, may not adjust to the heat because their heart can’t beat faster, Rao said.</p><p>The heat is also particularly dangerous for people who have taken a substance, ranging from alcohol to drugs. In David Sopys’ case, an autopsy determined he had taken two medications typically used to treat mental health conditions, and traces of cocaine were also found.</p><p>Cocaine is one of the substances that disrupts how the body distributes the blood to cool down the central organs, Rao said.</p><p>“It also makes your heart rate go fast, and then your heart rate’s already going fast from the heat so it’s too much for your heart to handle,” Rao said.</p><p>People experiencing homelessness are also more vulnerable to dehydration and heat stress, said Qi “Charles” Zhang, clinical director for the Street Medicine Institute, a nonprofit providing health care to the<b> </b>homeless across the country.</p><p>“The body is already under stress because they’re unhoused and they don’t get regular meals, and on top of it, they don’t have regular access to clean water,” Zhang said.</p><h3>Shelter during extreme weather</h3><p>As the Chicago area underwent a four-day stretch with temperatures climbing into the 90s in early September, the city’s Garfield Community Service Center, a cooling center on the West Side, sat nearly empty during one of those mornings. Inside a community room lined with blue plastic chairs, two people waited to talk to a case worker about housing. Plastic water bottles were placed at a table near the entrance.</p><p>Other cooling centers are even more underutilized. The South Chicago Center, 8650 S. Commercial Ave., and the Trina Davila Community Service Center, 4312 W. North Ave., each logged just three visitors during the heat wave from June 29 to July 3, according to records from the city’s Department of Family and Support Services.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-400000" name="image-400000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d9a7a7a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc8%2F5b%2Fc026a3134fcaae4f832a5e14c09b%2Fheatdeaths-garfield-jpeg.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d44c423/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc8%2F5b%2Fc026a3134fcaae4f832a5e14c09b%2Fheatdeaths-garfield-jpeg.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/813834a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc8%2F5b%2Fc026a3134fcaae4f832a5e14c09b%2Fheatdeaths-garfield-jpeg.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="The Garfield Center at 10 S. Kedzie Ave. is pictured on Sept. 2, 2026. The Garfield Center is one of the places the city of Chicago uses as a cooling facility during extreme weather events." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/813834a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc8%2F5b%2Fc026a3134fcaae4f832a5e14c09b%2Fheatdeaths-garfield-jpeg.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0d7e1c3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc8%2F5b%2Fc026a3134fcaae4f832a5e14c09b%2Fheatdeaths-garfield-jpeg.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/813834a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc8%2F5b%2Fc026a3134fcaae4f832a5e14c09b%2Fheatdeaths-garfield-jpeg.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The Garfield Center, 10 S. Kedzie Ave., is pictured on Sept. 2, 2026, when the city was experiencing a four-day stretch of abnormally hot and humid temperatures. The Garfield Center is one of the places the city of Chicago uses as a cooling facility during extreme weather events.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Elvia Malagón/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>It’s unclear if any of the people who died this summer tried to access a cooling center. David Sopys was among those who were found on the street. Another person, Stephanie Rodriguez, was found unresponsive at a bus stop before she was taken to an area hospital, according to records from the medical examiner.</p><p>Chicago Street Medicine, which does medical outreach to encampments and public transit stations, has been in talks with city officials about improving accessibility of cooling centers, said Alexa Canning, vice president of operations for the group. They’ve urged the city to open a static 24-hour location when temperatures go beyond 95 degrees or below 30 degrees, she said.</p><p>“We’ve seen that some of our patients have attempted to go to these warming and cooling centers and haven’t been able to access it for staffing issues or the sites are just closed,” Canning said, adding that they are also working to get information to patients since some don’t have access to the internet.</p><p>The city also faces a funding crunch to expand these types of services amid cuts to federal programs and grants, said Ald. Maria Hadden (49th).</p><p>“We’ve been looking to sustain what we have while we look for money to expand access,” Hadden said. “I think that there’s a conversation to be had, and we are having it, to pull in some of our business and philanthropic communities during this really challenging time under this federal administration.”</p><h3>Reducing emergency room visits during the heat</h3><p>Hadden pushed in September for an ordinance to provide <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2025/09/03/protect-workers-deadly-heat-summer-city-council-maria-hadden-michael-rodriguez" target="_blank" ><u>protections for outdoor workers</u></a> during periods of extreme heat. But Hadden said they have so far faced opposition from the business and hospitality industries.</p><p>She was behind the city’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2026/09/16/chicago-heatwave-cooling-ordinance-violation-air-conditioning-heat-related-death" target="_blank" ><u>cooling ordinance</u></a> that calls for certain buildings to provide air conditioning in every unit or maintain an air-conditioned common area when the heat exceeds 80 degrees. But some of those who died this summer without air conditioning lived in homes or apartments that aren’t covered by the ordinance.</p><p>“I do think the next step would be a cooling requirement ordinance for everyone, right,” Hadden said. “We don’t currently have that legislation in place … with the experiences that we’re seeing with our highest number of heat-related deaths this year that we’ve seen in a long time, I think we do need something like that.”</p><p>Extreme heat was also found to be behind even more health issues like skin conditions and even traffic accidents, according to a Northwestern University study published this summer in <a class="Link" href="https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aed3977" target="_blank" ><u>Science Advances</u></a>.</p><p>The study looked at electronic hospital records for emergency room visits in Chicago to analyze how climate impacts health outcomes. The younger population were more likely to come in for external conditions while older individuals experienced health concerns like swelling, leg ulcers and kidney issues, said Peter Graffy, a postdoctoral fellow at the University of Chicago.</p><p>Dr. Abel Kho, professor of medicine at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, said their data and research could be used to create climate adaptive healthcare, in which electronic records could pinpoint who is most at risk during a heat wave so that they could take preventative measures.</p><p>“The ideal situation is you would see no spike at all during heat events because everyone knew it was coming,” said Kho, one of the study’s authors. “And they knew that they were at risk and they did the appropriate things, and it would look no different than any other day.”</p><p></p><h3>‘My brother’s keeper’</h3><p>Tanja Sopys said Chicago officers patrolling neighborhoods could do more to pass out water or check for people showing signs of heat stress. But she said the city also needs deeper investments for community mental health services.</p><p>Tanja Sopys said her brother, who lived with mental health conditions, was never able to independently live on his own, transitioning from the care of their mother to their grandmother and then to her, the big sister. He bounced around different facilities, but he was never given a long-term solution, she said.</p><p>“Everybody that dealt with my brother was so eager to put him out, let him go,” she said.</p><p>Three months after her brother’s death, anxiety fills her whenever she drives near where he was found. Inside her living room, his black urn, decorated with his photo, is displayed on a bookshelf. She memorialized her brother in a video titled “my brother’s keeper,” showing photos of him at family gatherings.</p><p>The two were overprotective of each other, she said. Whenever she felt down, David Sopys would sit next to her and that was enough to comfort her.</p><p>“I keep seeing him walk down the street,” she said. “Somebody just walking, I keep thinking that he’s going to come and ring the doorbell. And if I see somebody that looks like him, it’s just still there.”</p>

entries.title: Chicago is getting a self-cleaning public restroom. Where is it, and when can it be used?
entries.summary: <p>The West Town neighborhood now has the city's first public toilet. </p><p>It's just not open for use yet. Ald. Daniel La Spata's (1st) office did not have an estimated completion date for when the toilet will be installed since the project was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2025/10/23/free-self-cleaning-public-toilet-la-spata" target="_blank" >announced last October</a>. But it has raised questions about how it will work, be managed, and who will pay for it. </p><p>Here's what you need to know.</p><h3>Where can I find the toilet?</h3><p>Chicago's sole public bathroom popped up this week near the CTA Blue Line station in the Polish Triangle at Division Street and Ashland and Milwaukee Avenues in West Town. Foundation work at the site is complete and contractors are working to attach utilities before restoration of the immediate area begins, according to La Spata’s office.</p><h3>How does it work?</h3><p>The public toilets like the one in West Town are free to use, but have a time limit and are automatically cleaned between uses. A combination of water and disinfectant is sprayed across the floor to clean anything left behind. Two toilet bowls are then rotated out to be disinfected by a power wash system.</p><p>Newer models can clean in 30 seconds, according to the French company JCDecaux, though older models took up to five minutes to disinfect between uses.</p><p> </p><h3>Who produces the toilet? Who is paying for it?</h3><p>JCDecaux, a French outdoor advertising company, is providing the restroom and maintenance at no cost to the city through a pilot program. However, the more than $400,000 in plumbing and installation costs will be covered with the 1st Ward’s menu funds — which City Council members receive annually for infrastructure projects in their ward — according to La Spata's office.</p><p>The company currently holds a three-year, $700,000 contract with the CTA through October 2027 to install and maintain screens displaying arrival times at city bus stations, which is an extension of previous contracts dating as far back as 2002, according to city records.</p><p>In addition to Chicago, JCDecaux has previously supplied 25 standalone public toilets <a class="Link" href="https://sfpublicworks.org/calendar/san-francisco-public-works-launches-new-jcdecaux-public-toilet-embarcadero-plaza" target="_blank" >to San Francisco</a> since 1994, and New York has seven already installed with plans to bring that number to 40 total. Last year, the company replaced 417 of the 435 self-cleaning restrooms it had installed in Paris with newer models. It also maintains 278 of the restrooms in Berlin that are among the 2,500 toilets it manages globally.</p><p>In San Francisco, the company signed a 20-year agreement to take on the full cost of design, manufacturing, installation and daily maintenance of toilets in exchange for installing <a class="Link" href="https://sfpublicworks.org/calendar/san-francisco-public-works-launches-new-jcdecaux-public-toilet-embarcadero-plaza" target="_blank" >114 advertising screens and kiosks</a> around the city.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-4e0000" name="image-4e0000"></a> <picture class="Figure-credit"><p>JCDecaux</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Why is there a public toilet need?</h3><p>Chicago, like many other cities, has struggled with bathroom access. A 2021 <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2021/10/21/chicagos-public-bathrooms-find-one-near-you-with-this-searchable-map/" target="_blank" >report</a> by the Chicago Tribune identified fewer than 500 structures in the city with free public restrooms, with most located in libraries, police stations, parks and other public buildings.</p><p>Officials globally have noted that the lack of public restrooms is particularly a problem for parents of young children, pregnant people, seniors, people with medical conditions and unhoused people. JCDecaux has supported the idea that access to hygiene is a human right.</p><p>New York is among several cities to have taken steps to <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/nyc-public-restrooms-toilets-parks-google-2cb515f49770f0bd65e68c2e5202324a" target="_blank" >spruce up its own public restrooms</a> in recent years. La Spata, who has been pushing for the toilets alongside Ald. Rossana Rodriguez Sanchez (33rd) for years, previously said it was something Chicago was "catching up" on.</p><h3>What are concerns over public restrooms?</h3><p>Some residents have voiced concerns that the public restrooms could attract crime or they would not be adequately cleaned. Those were similar issues JCDecaux faced and has begun to tackle in its other locations, the advertising giant said. </p><p>According to the San Francisco Chronicle, after a single bathroom in San Francisco racked up <a class="Link" href="https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/toilet-bathroom-san-francisco-22380080.php" target="_blank" >more than 200 maintenance requests</a> in less than four years of operation, the company began staffing and adapting the restrooms. </p><p>That city's public works department said JCDecaux spends about $2.2 million per year maintaining a full fleet of public restrooms and staffing an attendant at each of them seven days a week from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. "to ensure the toilets are kept safe, clean and operational."</p><p>It's unclear if Chicago's version will have an attendant.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2025/10/23/free-self-cleaning-public-toilet-la-spata" >Chicago’s first self-cleaning public toilet coming to the Northwest Side next year, alderperson says</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
entries.author: Violet Miller

entries.title: White Sox-Guardians playoff series can't get much closer than regular-season series
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — One game separated the Guardians and White Sox in the regular-season standings, and that’s exactly how close they were head-to-head. That figures to make for a nip-and-tuck playoff series in which one mistake could turn the tide.</p><p>“I think there's been four walk-offs,” Sox outfielder/designated hitter Randal Grichuk said Saturday before Game 1 of the American League Division Series (noon, TBS, truTV, 1000-AM). “And every game I feel like has been tight.</p><p>“We know every pitch, at-bat is going to matter. Every base, run is going to matter. So taking care of the baseball on defense and playing next-man-up mentality offensively is going to be huge for us.”</p><p>The Sox won the season series 7-6, giving them the tiebreaker should they have caught the Guardians for first place in the AL Central. But after losing two of three to the Guardians in mid-September, the Sox fell one game back after an 11-8 loss to the Tigers on Sept. 18 in which they blew a six-run lead. They never were in first place again.</p><p>The Sox outscored the Guardians 58-57 in the season series, with seven of the 13 games decided by one run. Four games were decided by two or three runs, and one was decided by four. The only blowout was an 8-2 Guardians victory.</p><p>“It really has been crazy kind of the back and forth that we’ve had all year,” Sox manager Will Venable said Friday. “We’re excited about the opportunity to play these guys, but we know full well how challenging it is to beat them. They're going to take advantage of every mistake that we make, whether that’s walks, giving them extra bases.”</p><p>The teams know each other so well that there probably isn’t anything either can do to surprise the other. This isn’t football, where a trick play can make a difference.</p><p>“It’s about executing game plans,” Venable said. “I think at this point, there's not some big adjustment in game plan that we have up our sleeve that we can throw at them. It’s about the guys executing, probably as much as any matchup that we've had where, as far as strategically, we know what we want to do on our side, they know what they want to do on their side.”</p>
entries.author: Jeff Agrest

entries.title: White Sox set roster, Game 1 lineup for ALDS matchup against division-rival Guardians
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND – White Sox manager Will Venable praised the energy that rookie outfielder Sam Antonacci brought to the top of the lineup during the Wild Card Series in Houston. But with the 2026 White Sox, energy does not come before platoon matchups, and Antonacci had a .604 OPS against left-handers this season.</p><p>Facing Guardians’ left-handed ace Parker Messick to start the American League Division Series, the White Sox are hoping this Chase Meidroth fellow can provide a spark of his own. Hagen Smith will be the first man on the mound of a likely bullpen game for the Sox.</p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-72720740-bf3a-11f1-97e1-c175e5eb8afe" start="1"><li>Chase Meidroth, 2B</li><li>Randal Grichuk, LF</li><li>Miguel Vargas, 3B</li><li>Munetaka Murakami, 1B</li><li>Tommy Pham, DH</li><li>Brenton Doyle, CF</li><li>Kyle Teel, C</li><li>Braden Montgomery, RF</li><li>Colson Montgomery, SS</li></ol><p>“Antonacci setting the tone and pounding his fist on his helmet is great,” said Venable. “Certainly he embodies the spirit of the club and is a good representative of the identity of the club. But there's other guys that feed into that too.”</p><p>The presence of Murakami and Braden Montgomery (rather than Luisangel Acuna and Tristan Peters) are only changes in personnel from the lineup the Sox threw at Messick on Sept. 16 in this same ballpark. Pham launched a three-run homer that briefly put the Sox ahead, but those were the only runs Messick allowed in six innings, en route to a 6-3 Guardians victory.</p><h3>Right-handed pitchers</h3><p><b>Sean Burke, Tyler Davis, Erick Fedde, Jordan Hicks, Davis Martin, David Sandlin and Grant Taylor</b></p><p>The only change on the ALDS roster from the Wild Card series is the Sox swapping out Huascar Brazoban and adding rookie right-hander Tyler Davis. Brazoban made a single appearance against the Astros and retired one of the three hitters he faced, but Venable said the decision was driven by Davis profiling as more platoon-neutral against a lefty-heavy Guardians roster.</p><h3>Left-handed pitchers</h3><p><b>Bryan Hudson, Anthony Kay, Sean Newcomb, Noah Schultz and Hagen Smith</b></p><p>No one in this group is likely to make a traditional start, or even work longer than three innings. But with only three true right-handed hitters on the Guardians roster (Austin Hedges, Jo Adell, David Fry), every Sox southpaw should be plenty busy throughout the ALDS.</p><h3>Catchers</h3><p><b>Jake Rogers and Kyle Teel</b></p><p>As his presence in the starting lineup against Messick indicates, Teel should catch every inning of this series unless something surprising happens.</p><h3>Infielders</h3><p><b>Luisangel Acuña, Chase Meidroth, Colson Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Miguel Vargas</b></p><p>Vargas and Murakami scuffled to a combined 1-for-17 showing in Houston and it’s a testament to the Sox roster that they put up 13 runs on the Astros in two games in spite of it. They almost certainly cannot top the Guardians with a repeat of such a performance.</p><h3>Outfielders</h3><p><b>Sam Antonacci, Andrew Benintendi, Brenton Doyle, Randal Grichuk, Braden Montgomery, Tristan Peters and Tommy Pham.</b></p><p>Doyle is the only one of four players the White Sox acquired at the trade deadline to make their ALDS roster, and coaches are encouraged by how his remodeled swing has looked recently. Before going 1-for-2 with a single in the Wild Card series, Doyle had a .927 OPS in September.</p>

entries.title: Man fatally shot during Belmont Cragin break-in
entries.summary: <p>A man was shot and killed during a home invasion in Belmont Cragin early Saturday, police said.</p><p>The man, 60, was inside an apartment in the 3000 block of North Lotus Avenue around 5:20 a.m. when someone entered the back door and fired shots, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man was pronounced dead on the scene and the gunman fled.</p><p>No other injuries were reported and detectives are investigating.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: City of Chicago plans to fill thousands of potholes Saturday in 'repair blitz'
entries.summary: <p>The city's transportation department is stepping up its street repairs and planning to fill thousands of potholes Saturday.</p><p>More than 30 Department of Transportation crews will hit the streets with a goal of filling more than 5,000 potholes around the city, Mayor Brandon Johnson said in a press release. It's the second consecutive weekend of the "repair blitz," and crews tackled nearly 5,600 potholes last Saturday.</p><p>"Every pothole we fill makes our streets safer and more accessible for the people who rely on them every day," Johnson said in the release. "This weekend, Chicagoans will see the full force of government at work, with crews working across the city to ensure we are preparing our streets for the winter months ahead. I’m incredibly grateful for the CDOT crews and public servants who never waver in their dedication to improving the lives of their neighbors while building the Chicago we all deserve.” </p><p>Crews are prepping for winter, the worst season for potholes around the city, by proactively addressing some of the worst areas for run-down streets, the release said.</p><p>“CDOT is working hard to deliver the quality-of-life improvements that residents count on, from filling potholes to resurfacing neighborhood streets,” CDOT Commissioner William Cheaks said in the release. “We know street conditions matter to everyone who travels through our neighborhoods, and we’re making the most of the fall construction season to get this work done. I want to thank our crews for their dedication and the hard work they put in every day to keep Chicago moving.”</p><p>Residents can report potholes by calling 311, using the CHI311 app or visiting <a class="Link" href="http://311.chicago.gov/" target="_blank" ><u>311.chicago.gov</u></a>.</p>

entries.title: University of Chicago's South Side Science Festival returns
entries.summary: <p>Thousands of kids and adults stepped into the white coats of University of Chicago students and researchers on Saturday for the fifth annual South Side Science Festival.</p><p>More than 130 hands-on demonstrations and activities ranging in disciplines from biology, aerospace, physics and more spanned the campus, allowing children and adults to play games, conduct experiments and ask questions of professional scientists.</p><p>The South Side Science Festival was inspired by The Long Night of Sciences — a public science festival in Germany where universities and research labs open their doors to the public. Organizers say the event intends to close the gap between the South Side community and researchers by demonstrating that science is for everyone.</p><p>“We wanted to replicate [The Long Night of Sciences festival],” said Maanasa Raghavan, associate professor in the Department of Human Genetics and a founding organizer. “But at the same time, make it very focused on our communities here on the south side.”</p><p>Raghavan says polarizing opinions about the role of science professionals and federal funding cuts in science can be demoralizing, but seeing thousands of people engaging at their annual festival is a reminder of how important their work is.</p><p>“We may be fostering young scientists,” she said. “That's why we're here, and we'll keep showing up.”</p><p>Organizer Luke Dyer says the festival was also a direct response to general fears and distrust in medicine following the initial COVID-19 outbreak.</p><p>“The idea is to bring people in and show them the science that's happening [at the University of Chicago], and also answer their questions,” he said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure As a researcher, she says she can spend upwards of 60 hours a week researching and running experiments, but volunteering at the festival drives her to do better work.</p><p>“These long, hard days of doing experiments — you come out here, you see what matters to people, it grounds us really,” Bessiake said.</p><p>She loves experiencing the moment it all clicks: where people begin to understand how and why scientists do what they do.</p><p>“The kids are playing with slime — they’re also asking questions,” Bessiake said. “And they're like, ‘Oh, that's why I should get vaccinated.’”</p><p>South suburb resident Nijel Mottley said his 4 year-old son loves mixing things and watching science shows on YouTube.</p><p>“He's pretty hands-on so he’s really enjoying it,” Mottley said.</p><p>Mottley brought his son, Remy, to the festival to foster his interest in science.</p><p>“We need more scientists to solve these issues, and this kind of fosters that and allows them to learn the different ways science can be applied,” Mottley said.</p>

entries.title: Notre Dame, Carr run past Bill Belichick's Tar Heels
entries.summary: <p>CHAPEL HILL, N.C. — CJ Carr threw for four touchdowns and ran for another and third-ranked Notre Dame leaned on its ground game in regaining control after halftime to beat North Carolina 37-26 on Saturday.</p><p>The Fighting Irish (5-0) were on the verge of going up 28-7 before the Tar Heels (2-2) came up with a goal-line stand and turned it into a long touchdown drive right before halftime. Then UNC came out of the break with Jaden Jefferson sprinting through the rain for a 98-yard kickoff return that brought the Tar Heels to within 21-20.</p><p>That's when Carr and the Irish offense went to work with a series of methodical and physical drives, leaning on the run in wet conditions to carry the ball right into the heart of the defensive front and consistently move the chains. That ultimately helped Notre Dame restore its multiple-possession lead while finishing with a season-high 241 yards on the ground.</p><p>“When they know you're going to try to run the ball — and you're still able to run the ball — because of the weather conditions, that's a reflection of your team, and the toughness and the physicality,” coach Marcus Freeman said.</p><p>Notre Dame responded to Jefferson's big play with a 17-play, 75-yard drive lasting more than nine minutes by the time Carr got around the right side for a fourth-down TD keeper.</p><p>Then, after forcing a three-and-out, Notre Dame went to work again in pummeling fashion. Nolan James Jr. did most of the work on the ground, then caught Carr's short pass in the left flat and juked a would-be tackler off his feet to go in for a 6-yard TD and a 34-20 lead to open the fourth quarter.</p><p>Freshman Jonaz Walton posted a team-high 120 yards to lead Notre Dame's ground effort, while James added 65. The Irish's rushing output included 122 yards in the third quarter alone in stymieing UNC's momentum, a welcome sign for a new ground game that lost running backs Jeremiyah Love and Jadarian Price as first-round NFL draft picks.</p><p>“Super impressive with the way the offensive line kind of just drove the ball down the field,” Carr said. “They couldn't really stop us. It felt like we were imposing our will on them whenever we wanted to.”</p><p>Carr threw for 234 yards, with Jordan Faison making eight catches for 132 yards and two scores.</p><p>Billy Edwards Jr. threw for three touchdowns for the Tar Heels but was picked off twice. North Carolina also struggled to get anything going on the ground (77 yards on 23 carries).</p><p>“We were certainly competitive, we missed some opportunities,” coach Bill Belichick said. “We just need to do a better job of coaching and playing, take advantage of those opportunities.”</p><p><b>The takeaway</b></p><p>Notre Dame: The defense had its hiccups in the Fighting Irish's 15th straight win. The Irish entered Saturday ranked No. 1 nationally by surrendering 199.3 yards per game and second in scoring (8.3), yet the Tar Heels came within seven points of matching the total the Irish had allowed through four games.</p><p>UNC: The Tar Heels started 2-0 before blowing a two-touchdown lead in a loss at Clemson on Sept. 19, then had an open week to prepare for this one. Finding ways to generate more downfield passing gains was a focus, and Edwards found more success. The primary targets were wideout Jordan Shipp (seven catches for 109 yards) and Jelani Thurman (five catches for 50 yards and two TDs) as the Tar Heels flirted with a marquee win in Belichick's second season.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Notre Dame: The Fighting Irish host Stanford next Saturday.</p><p>UNC: The Tar Heels visit Pittsburgh next Saturday, the first of back-to-back road games against teams that are a combined 9-0.</p>
entries.author: AP

entries.title: Barrington shuts out Conant, continues its midseason surge
entries.summary: <p>Barrington’s football community has always stood out from others around the area, especially in the northern suburbs. The Broncos’ annual success seemed to come from longtime coach Joe Sanchez and an extremely supportive local atmosphere.</p><p>So it was surprising to hear the Barrington players felt their fans turned on them during their winless start to the season. The Broncos lost to Lyons, Lincoln-Way Central, Naperville North and Hersey after opening the year in the preseason Super 25 rankings.</p><p>“Everyone said Barrington fell off,” senior linebacker Owen Nichols said.</p><p>“Our fans and other friends all didn’t believe in us,” junior running back Lamar Osterhues said. “We had a phrase on our team: ‘stay on that side.’ We have our family right here. We know what we can do. We came in every week on Monday and believed in each other.”</p><p>Things are turning around for Barrington now. The Broncos have won three consecutive games after shutting out visiting Conant 42-0 on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/10/01/high-school-football-scores-week-7" >Saturday</a>.</p><p>“If I am being honest, I don’t really pay much attention [to what the fans are saying],” Sanchez said. “We have enough of our own issues here. We just have to focus on us. Certainly it was an atypical start for us. I’ve been here 31 years. Twenty-five as the head coach. We haven’t played that tough of a four-game stretch at the beginning of the year ever. Those were four great teams. And we were young, and we had some injuries.”</p><p>Sanchez and Osterhues both credited the scout team, nicknamed “The Dirty Show,” for helping Barrington get its season back on track.</p><p>“We have a great senior group that didn’t give in and kept fighting,” Sanchez said. “I am proud of our kids and our coaches and excited that we get some more meaningful games in October.”</p><p>Barrington’s defensive line dominated the first half and even scored a touchdown when lineman Cru Lucier fell on the ball in the end zone after Duke Matiyow blocked a Conant punt.</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: Woman in custody after girl, 7, fatally stabbed in Chatham
entries.summary: <p>A 7-year-old girl died after being stabbed in the Chatham neighborhood Saturday, police said.</p><p>The girl was walking outside in the 8600 block of South Cottage Grove Avenue just before noon when a woman approached her and stabbed her multiple times in the back, according to Chicago police. </p><p>Bystanders noticed the stabbing and intervened, detaining the woman, police said.</p><p>The girl was taken to Comer Children's Hospital, where she was pronounced dead.</p><p>The woman suffered injuries during the scuffle with bystanders, and she was taken to the hospital and taken into police custody.</p><p>Detectives are investigating.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Bears put left tackle Braxton Jones on injured reserve, elevate DE Marcus Davenport for Jets game
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> put left tackle Braxton Jones on injured reserve Saturday, ruling him out for the next four games. Jones already was set to miss the game Sunday against the Jets and now can’t return until the Nov. 2 game against the Seahawks.</p><p>Backup swing tackle Theo Benedet took over for Jones when he hurt his knee Monday against the Eagles and will start against the Jets. The Bears could pivot to backup Jordan McFadden or move left guard Joe Thuney to left tackle if he struggles.</p><p>The Bears are hopeful to get former second-round pick Ozzy Trapilo back soon, but have been careful not to rush his recovery from a major knee injury. Coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >Ben Johnson</a> was optimistic about him returning, but said Friday it wouldn’t be for this game.</p><p>“We’re still working out Ozzy just to make sure that the confidence is back,” Johnson said. “He’s looking better each and every week.”</p><p>The Bears play at the Packers next week, then visit the Falcons.</p><p>They also elevated defensive end Marcus Davenport and cornerback Nick McCloud from their practice squad. That’s a big development for Davenport, who joined the team Aug. 17 and has been working his way into shape. He has 25 career sacks in 77 games.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Munetaka Murakami's early two-run blast powers White Sox over Guardians 3-0 in Game 1
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND – The last time the White Sox faced the Guardians and their ace rookie Parker Messick at Progressive Field, a Tommy Pham three-run homer was the only damage they could muster in a 6-3 loss.</p><p>In a 3-0 victory to open up their best-of-five American League Division Series showdown against the AL Central champions on Saturday, Sox pitching flattened the Guardians' offense enough to make three runs look like plenty, even after an initially apparent Pham three-run blast in the sixth evaporated into an odd-looking double play.</p><p>After a combined 1-for-17 showing in the Wild Card series versus Houston, close friends Miguel Vargas and Munetaka Murakami bested those contributions in the fourth alone. Murakami followed a sharp leadoff single from Vargas by swatting an elevated Parker Messick sinker on the inner-third 440 feet to the outer reaches of the right field concourse to stake the White Sox to a 2-0 lead they never relinquished.</p><p>Batting in the ninth spot as he has all postseason to this point, Colson Montgomery added insurance with his second seeing-eye grounder of the day in the seventh. Facing fellow lefty Erik Sabrowski, Montgomery softly poked a grounder down the third-base line against a Guardians defense playing him to pull. Kyle Teel raced all the way around from first as Cleveland’s defense scrambled in pursuit.</p><p>Hagen Smith’s start mirrored his scoreless three innings last round against Houston for the first eight outs. But as he was a strike away from finishing off the third in less than 40 total pitches, he lost his control and issued three straight walks. Bryan Hudson engineered an escape by inducing a full-count fly out from outfielder Chase DeLauter, but a similar jam emerged in the fourth.</p><p>Jordan Hicks struck out the first two hitters before allowing a two-out walk to pinch-hitter Nathaniel Lowe. When Anthony Kay emerged to face fellow lefty Travis Bazzana, he allowed a double, and walked Austin Hedges to load the bases before getting Brayan Rocchio to softly line out to right and strand three Guardians baserunners again. Cleveland only enjoyed three at-bats with runners in scoring position.</p><p>It certainly looked like Tommy Pham had added some cushion when a fly ball sizzled off his bat at 106.1 mph with two runners on in the sixth, and both Pham and Miguel Vargas reacted in kind. But a stiff wind knocked it down enough for Angel Martinez to make a leaping catch at the left field wall — which held up on a replay challenge. Vargas was easily doubled off first while Pham stood flabbergasted at how a ball he struck so cleanly produced such a result.</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Raucous reception awaits Patrick Kane in Blackhawks' home opener Tuesday, even if it's 'unknown' to him
entries.summary: <p>BUFFALO, N.Y. — Patrick Kane claims he's unsure what the atmosphere will be like for his Tuesday return to the United Center with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>.</p><p>"When I went back there for my first game [there with] Detroit, you don't really know what the reception is going to be or how it's going to play out," Kane said Saturday. "That's the fun part about it. </p><p>"There's probably going to be some excitement, [but] it's just the unknown of what's going to happen and what it's going to be like. I can't wait."</p><p>Well, I have a pretty good idea what it will be like: raucous.</p><p>Kane might not be as acutely aware of this fact as he would be if the Hawks hadn't traded him in 2023, but Hawks fans have had preciously few in-the-present moments to enjoy and celebrate lately. </p><p>They've had no choice but to turn to nostalgia for satisfaction — especially during the franchise's yearlong centennial celebration last season — while waiting for the return of on-ice success.</p><p>And the mere thought of Kane, arguably the greatest player in franchise history and arguably the greatest American hockey player ever, has consistently conjured up the most vivid, proud, triumphant nostalgia of all within the fan base.</p><p>Seeing Kane in the flesh elevates that to another level. The seemingly endless standing ovation he received in his aforementioned return <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2024/02/25/patrick-kane-overtime-goal-red-wings-blackhawks-nhl-return-chicago-alex-debrincat" >with the Red Wings</a> in February 2024 — two minutes that felt like two hours — demonstrated that phenomenon.</p><p>So seeing Kane in the flesh wearing a Hawks sweater again? That will be downright euphoric for the 20,000-some fans who will flock to Madison Street for the team's home opener. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/dEU39vLtAfU?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="GOTTA SEE IT: Patrick Kane Receives Lengthy Standing Ovation In Return To Chicago"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>No matter how this season goes — or how next season goes, for that matter, since Kane is on a two-year contract — his place in Hawks fans' hearts will never change. He earned that permanent real estate long ago, and it truly is permanent.</p><p>He could put a cherry on top of his iconic Chicago legacy, though, if he somehow helps push this young Hawks team back into contention. There is a new forward-looking element to the Kane hullabaloo that didn't exist in 2024.</p><p>And despite the Hawks' ugly opening week, Kane still sounds optimistic about the trajectory.</p><p>"I know we haven't started off great this year, but I think there's a lot of potential in the room," he said. "I think could be a winning team here pretty soon."</p><p>The fact Kane chose to sign with the Hawks this summer after weeks of deliberating between them and his hometown Sabres — who already became winners again last season — says something about his belief in the Hawks' young core.</p><p>Kane has always <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/17/blackhawks-patrick-kane-right-decision" >gravitated</a> toward young players who share his passion for spending as much time on the ice as possible, and there are plenty of guys like that on this team.</p><p>Some of them are closer in age to Kane's five-year-old son Patrick Jr. than they are to 37-year-old Kane himself.</p><p>As those Hawks youngsters attempt to maintain confidence through this early-season adversity, which they crucially need to do long enough to find their NHL sea legs and start gathering some positive momentum, Kane's aura and experience could be beneficial.</p><p>"Patrick's presence helps our team in general, just with the belief that he has — when he comes to the rink every day — that he's going to be a great player and that the team is going to win," coach Jeff Blashill said. </p><p>"That's a positive thing. But I also think it'd be a lot to ask him to necessarily be responsible for other guys' confidence. Individually, you have to pick yourself up. I think true confidence comes from within. Each guy has to make sure they come with that belief that they're going to be a great player and we're going to be a really good hockey team."</p>
entries.author: Ben Pope

entries.title: Man visiting from upstate New York shot during attempted robbery in Streeterville
entries.summary: <p>Two suspects are in police custody after a man visiting from upstate New York with his wife was shot during an attempted robbery while in a Streeterville parking garage Friday evening.</p><p>The attack happened about 6:30 p.m. in the 400 block of East Illinois Street as the man, 64, and his wife, 29, of Plattsburgh, were retrieving something from their rental car in a lower level of a garage, according to a police report obtained by the Sun-Times.</p><p>Witnesses told police two masked robbers confronted the couple, and one demanded the man give him his keys while brandishing a black gun in their direction, according to the report.</p><p>When the man refused, the gunman reportedly said, “Give me your keys, or I’m going to shoot you,” before he opened fire, hitting the man in the left side of his rib cage, according to the report.</p><p>Police and paramedics responding to the scene slowed the man's bleeding after he was found lying on the ground. He was taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital, according to the report. </p><p>Meanwhile, the two attackers fled the parking garage through the Grand Avenue exit and headed west, the report said.</p><p>Charges have not been announced for the suspects, one of whom is 16 and the other 22, who were in police custody, according to the report.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Four offseason questions facing Jed Hoyer, Cubs, who have pitching at top of lengthy to-do list
entries.summary: <p>As baseball’s postseason marches on, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> are forced to start their offseason work much earlier than hoped.</p><p>Expectations won’t change for 2027; this will still be a team with World Series goals.</p><p>But <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/10/02/cubs-jed-hoyer-offseason-mlb-free-agents-postseason-playoffs-padres-starting-pitching-rotation" >Jed Hoyer’s front office has a lot to do</a> to make next year’s team better equipped than the one that was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/10/01/cubs-playoffs-loss-mlb-postseason-2027-mlb-offseason-free-agency-jed-hoyer-craig-counsell-alex-bregman-pete-crow-armstrong-ian-happ" >rapidly bounced from the playoffs</a>.</p><p>Here are four of the biggest questions facing Hoyer & Co.</p><h3><b>Will any starting pitchers return?</b></h3><p>Hoyer might have to replace his entire starting rotation, with lefties Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga and David Peterson, as well as righties Clay Holmes and Kevin Gausman, all likely heading to free agency.</p><p>Might any return?</p><p>“I’ve been very fortunate to be a Cub and to have had an opportunity to be part of this ballclub,” Boyd said last week. “I believe my best is still ahead of me. I hope it gets to be here.”</p><p>At one point, Holmes looked like a prime candidate to go from trade-deadline rental to rotation cornerstone, but he struggled down the stretch and didn’t pitch in the playoffs.</p><p>Hoyer still described Holmes as someone “who fits our team really well,” a ground-ball guy with the best defense in baseball behind him.</p><p>Regardless of whether any return, though, expect the Cubs to spend on arms this winter.</p><p>“It’s safe to say that the biggest part of our focus going into the offseason is going to be on pitching,” Hoyer said Friday. “Whether that’s 100-to-0, what that ratio is going to be, has not been determined yet. But certainly, the great majority of our focus is going to be on pitching acquisition going in.”</p><h3><b>Will there be another bullpen makeover?</b></h3><p>That pitching focus could also include a bullpen overhaul.</p><p>The Cubs signed a lot of relievers last winter, and it didn’t work out, certainly not the way it did in 2025, when the team’s back-end relief group was a strength.</p><p>“I did a poor job on the bullpen this year, full stop,” Hoyer said. “We didn’t get it right, and that’s something we’ve spent a lot of time talking about already and we’ll continue to talk about.</p><p>“I take responsibility for that, and it’s something we’ll look to improve on this offseason.”</p><p>Daniel Palencia, Phil Maton and Shelby Miller are under contract for next season, while the team has option decisions to make on Colin Rea, Javier Assad and Jacob Webb.</p><p>Given Hoyer’s poor self-evaluation, it seems anything is possible on that front.</p><h3><b>End of Cubs careers for Ian Happ, Seiya Suzuki?</b></h3><p>It’s not just pitching Hoyer will have to sort out.</p><p>Happ, the longest tenured Cub, is a free agent, and after a season that, statistically, did not match up with previous ones, whether he returns is a mystery.</p><p>That alone was enough to send Happ’s teammates to tears.</p><p>“He truly embodies what it means to wear the jersey,” shortstop Dansby Swanson said. “He embodies the Cubs more than anyone I know.”</p><p>“He is the Chicago Cubs,” center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong said.</p><p>Happ has seemingly braced himself for the potential end to a decade-long stay on the North Side.</p><p>“All I can say is that I love being a Cub,” Happ said. “I’ve loved my time. I’ve loved the place, the people, Wrigley Field, the fan base. And it’s been truly special. I don’t think there’s a better place in baseball to play.”</p><p>Hoyer spoke glowingly of Happ on Friday but forecasted coming conversations rather than a firm decision.</p><p>Suzuki, too, is a pending free agent after five Cubs seasons, expected to be among the top hitters on the market, potentially opening up another hole in the outfield.</p><h3><b>How good are in-house solutions?</b></h3><p>There are potential answers to these questions already on the roster.</p><p>But how good of solutions are they?</p><p>In the rotation, righties Cade Horton and Ben Brown, plus lefty Justin Steele, could make for an intriguing nucleus. But all three will be coming off significant injuries that wiped out most or all of their 2026s.</p><p>“It does prevent a bit of a team-building challenge,” Hoyer said. “All three guys have a real chance to impact us next year, but how much is a real question and we have to build accordingly.”</p><p>Two of this season’s reserves, utility man Matt Shaw and infielder Pedro Ramirez, could potentially help fill voids created by the departures of Happ and/or Suzuki.</p><p>The ability to backfill from within on that front would be helpful, should the Cubs allocate their resources with a focus on pitching.</p><p>“Having Pedro and Matt, super versatile, both really good players,” Hoyer said, “we can ask more of them going forward. We didn’t have to this year, given the nature of our corner outfield. But I think they both can certainly do that, and we’ll lean on both those guys more heavily going forward.”</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Loyola's defense steps up to shut down the St. Ignatius ground game
entries.summary: <p>Five plays into Saturday's game against St. Ignatius, No. 1 Loyola was in a seven-point hole.</p><p>The Hites brothers, quarterback Reid and receiver Connor, teamed up for a 64-yard touchdown pass and the Wolfpack had the best start they could hope for.</p><p>But then linebacker Will Mettee and the Ramblers defense went to work and it was all Loyola the rest of the way in a 38-7 win against No. 15 St. Ignatius.</p><p>Junior quarterback Matthew Lee's laserlike precision accounted for 244 yards and two touchdowns on 16 of 22 passing. He also ran for a score for Loyola (7-0). Aidan Collins (eight catches, 150 yards, TD) and Jordan McKinley (five catches, 113 yards) were Lee's top targets.</p><p>Melo Maldonado, another junior, had 56 yards and three touchdowns — two rushing, one receiving — on 14 touches.</p><p>That was way more offense than the Ramblers needed after the early defensive hiccup against the Wolfpack (5-2).</p><p>St. Ignatius' offense has confounded plenty of opponents with its blend of deception, misdirection and speed.</p><p>"Thankfully we have good coaches on the defensive side that put these guys in the right spot," Loyola coach John Holecek said. "We got an extra day [of practice] so we drilled them. But it's eye discipline and just looking at the keys and assignment football — if they do this, we have to do this.</p><p>"You can't get used to the speed of what they do early."</p><p>Mettee, a linebacker committed to Boston College, is the leader of the Ramblers defense and took charge after the Wolfpack touchdown.</p><p>"After that, I talked to my safety, making sure we were on the same page," he said. "We also went over that [in] halftime adjustments. But the rest of the game, I think our back end did really well, just taking their guys, staring at them and making sure they didn't have false eyes on their quarterback."</p><p>Reid Hites finished 2 of 6 passing for 82 yards. Sophomore fullback Nino Capuano had eight carries for 64 yards for St. Ignatius.</p><p>"I also think we defeated the dive pretty well," Mettee said. "Because [Capuano] is obviously a tough kid — small to the ground [at 5-7, 175 pounds] but he can stay up and he's a good player. For the next two years, he'll be rushing a lot."</p><p>The Wolfpack's second drive ended with a missed field goal and they didn't pass midfield again till late in the fourth quarter,</p><p>Meanwhile, Loyola's offense was humming along despite the absence of tight end Charlie Fowler, another Boston College commit, and receiver Brendan Fitzgerald.</p><p>Collins, who had been dealing with a leg injury, showed no ill effects. "His hands are great, he catches everything," Holecek said.</p><p>Lee's pinpoint throws made the receivers' jobs easy. And having targets like McKinley, a four-star junior prospect, and Collins make it hard for opposing defenses to cover everyone.</p><p>"Just get the ball in the athletes' hands and they get the job done," Lee said.</p><p>"He's growing and growing," Holecek said of Lee. "He's still young, he's halfway through his junior year and he's so much more poised in the pocket. The more he plays in this offense, the more comfortable he will be — knowing where to get the ball, where to look."<br></p>
entries.author: Mike Clark

entries.title: Aspiring paramedic recalls how a CTA bus seat dispute turned into shooting
entries.summary: <p>While several passengers scrambled toward the doors after two people were wounded in a shooting on a CTA bus Wednesday, Malik Nitz ran toward the danger. </p><p>Nitz, a 28-year-old who is an aspiring paramedic, saw an opportunity to help. </p><p>"My first response [after hearing the shot] was, 'Who got hit?'" Nitz told the Sun-Times. "Everyone was running off the bus, and I was running to the incident where the shot was fired." </p><p>Nitz found a 65-year-old woman who was struck in the arm and told her to remain calm before tending to a 57-year-old man who was wounded and collapsed after attempting to chase the shooter, he said. </p><p>"I didn't know if he was going to make it," said Nitz, who will soon start training to become a paramedic and used his general knowledge to treat the shooting victims. </p><p>. "I had to get like some tissue, some wrap or some napkins or something to stop the internal bleeding." </p><p>"I didn't want to press too hard on it because I didn't want to expand his wound," Nitz added. "So I applied light pressure to try to stop the bleeding. I ended up getting blood on my clothes, but I mean that's the least of my problems."</p><p>The injured man was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center in critical condition. The woman, struck in her left arm, was transported to the same hospital in fair condition, police said.</p><p>Nitz was on his way home from work when a man and woman began fighting with another passenger over a wet seat around 4:40 p.m. in the 300 block of West 63rd Street, according to Nitz and police reports obtained by the Sun-Times. </p><p>"Basically, the lady wanted him to get up, and he didn't want to get up, so she apparently got to swinging on him," Nitz said.</p><p>When the argument turned physical, the seated passenger reportedly pulled a gun and fired, authorities said. </p><p>Nitz noted that there were "a lot of scared people" on the bus, including several high school students. </p><p>"The children were running off the bus, and they were screaming at the top of their lungs," Nitz said. "The bus was very intense." </p><p>Estrelitta Harmon, executive director with the Center For Better Aging, called the shooting “unacceptable” and stressed the importance of including older adults in conversations about public safety.</p><p>The agency provides support resources — including transportation — to thousands of South Side residents over 50. </p><p>"Transportation is the largest social barrier to access to care, but it isn't just about connecting to healthcare," Harmon said. "It's about navigating throughout your life, about getting access to grocery stores or shopping or connecting with your family in your community. And so, so many of our older adults in the city rely on public transportation."</p><p>Harmon noted that safety on public transportation is extremely important, especially for the city's older population. </p><p>"The seniors in our community, they deserve to feel safe. They deserve to maintain their independence and participate fully in their communities," Harmon said. "I am hopeful that we will see a future where that exists for our entire population."</p>

entries.title: Did the White Sox run into an embarrassing double play, or were they victims of a statistical anomaly?
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND – With a different result in Game 1 of the American League Division Series, it’s an all-time embarrassing playoff moment for the White Sox.</p><p>With two on and one out in the sixth, <b>Tommy Pham</b> unloaded on a Erik Sabrowski fastball. Both he and the White Sox dugout reacted like a back-breaking three-run homer had been hit. <b>Miguel Vargas</b>, the team’s “best baserunner” per manager <b>Will Venable</b>, assumed it was at least a double off Progressive Field’s high left field wall, and had already rounded second when Guardians left fielder <b>Angel Martinez</b> made a leaping catch.</p><p>Vargas was easily doubled off to end the inning, Pham stared out in disbelief, and the White Sox burned a replay challenge that wound up confirming the catch. What a blunder.</p><p>Or was it an all-time aberrant result, which wound up not mattering in a 3-0 Sox triumph in Game 1?</p><p>“I've hit enough to know what is a homer, what should be a homer, and what isn't,” Pham told the Sun-Times. “Everybody in our dugout was confused there, [with] 106 mph pulled like that. I hit a ball here two weeks ago that went 420 feet that I hit similar to that. This ball I pulled it <i>more</i>.”</p><p>The 38-year-old Pham is experienced enough to know what a homer feels like, and data-savvy enough to know metrics back him up. His fly out checked in at 106.1 mph at a 31-degree angle. A Statcast search reveals that of the 82 balls hit 106 mph or harder at 31 degrees this year in MLB, 81 were home run. The 82nd was caught at the wall in dead center at Houston’s Daikin Park.</p><p>Even with an ugly result, baserunners are making split-second reads on contact quality, and Venable found it hard to take issue with how Vargas read such a drive.</p><p>“You don’t want that to happen, but you understand the read and trust the player,” Venable said. “I think every single person thought that that ball was at least halfway up the wall, if not a homer.”</p><p>Pham made a different type of peace with it, since the measured nine mph wind blowing right-to-left offered a less-than-satisfying explanation.</p><p>“I don’t know, it might’ve just been a dead ball,” Pham said. “Baseball gods will look out for me another time.”</p><p><b>Teel’s mad dash</b></p><p>Speaking of both Statcast and blessings from the baseball gods, before it began its roll down the third base line, <b>Colson Montgomery’s </b>seventh-inning RBI double left the bat at 64 mph; the fourth-slowest postseason extra-base hit since 2015.</p><p>With two outs, <b>Kyle</b> <b>Teel </b>was waved home from first on an aggressive send from third base coach Justin Jirschele.</p><p>“Jirsch always says, ‘scared money don't make money,’” said Venable. “When it's a low run scoring environment, we really needed it.”</p><p>It was needed, and also doesn’t work unless Guardians catcher <b>Austin Hedges</b> drops the throw from left field.</p><p>“I was dead at arrival,” admitted Teel, but that doesn’t mean he was shocked by the send. “Not at all. I’m fast.”</p><p><b>Rare air for Taylor</b></p><p>On Saturday, <b>Grant Taylor</b> became the sixth pitcher in MLB history to record a postseason save of four innings or more, and the first since <b>Lance McCullers </b>did it in Game 7 of the 2017 ALCS. That McCullers outing featured even more curveballs than the 16 Taylor threw.</p>

entries.title: Thousands attend Out of the Darkness Walk in commemoration of lives affected by suicide
entries.summary: <p>Thousands affected by suicide came together Saturday at Chicago’s Montrose Harbor for the Out of the Darkness Chicagoland Walk. </p><p>Each participant was asked to wear “honor beads,” representing a loved one they’ve lost. They wore white for a child, red for a spouse or partner, gold for a parent and purple for a friend. </p><p>The colorful beads, the sort of thing you’d ordinarily see at a Mardi Gras celebration, reflect an event that’s part festival, part somber commemoration.</p><p><i>This article references suicide. If you are in crisis, please call, text or chat with the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988<s>,</s> or contact the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741.</i></p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: Grant Taylor caps White Sox' latest bullpen game with four-inning save
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — Everyone thought that White Sox reliever Grant Taylor’s day was done after the eighth inning Saturday. He already had thrown 31 pitches through three innings, and Sean Newcomb had been warming up.</p><p>Even the official scorer in the Progressive Field press box mistakenly announced that Newcomb was entering the game in the ninth.</p><p>But he didn’t. Taylor went back out to finish the job.</p><p>“[Pitching coach] Zach Bove gave me a look I know kind of means, how do you feel, what do you got,” Taylor said. “And I gave him a nod.”</p><p>Taylor retired the Guardians’ 2-3-4 hitters — Jose Ramirez, Chase DeLauter and Jo Adell — with the greatest of ease, sealing the Sox’ 3-0 victory in Game 1 of the American League Division Series. He faced 13 batters, allowed two hits and struck out six in his first four-inning outing since 2024 at Single-A Kannapolis.</p><p>“I don't know what else to say about him,” manager Will Venable said. “He's a beast out there. “I thought he actually got better as that outing went on.”</p><p>“That’s the best I’ve probably seen anyone pitch,” catcher Kyle Teel said. “That was just unbelievable.”</p><p>It came four days after Taylor threw 54 pitches in 2 ⅓ innings to close out a Game 1 victory against the Astros in the wild-card series. Through three playoff game, guess who leads the Sox in innings pitched and batters faced. It’s Taylor, the guy finishing games, not starting them.</p><p>What the White Sox are doing with their pitching staff isn’t normal. For normal teams — you know, teams with a rotation — the starting pitcher goes, say, five, maybe even (gasp) six innings. It does happen.</p><p>“We would’ve liked to do that,” general manager Chris Getz said earlier in the week. “But if we were trying to win games, we had to lean on the strengths of the club, and we’ve done that.”</p><p>For the Sox, piecing together a plan to get 27 outs must be as tedious as doing your taxes. But it’s working. On Saturday, left-hander Hagen Smith started — or opened or commenced or got the ball rolling? — with 2 ⅔ innings. He retired the first eight batters he faced before walking three in a row. What happened?</p><p>“Sometimes it can be trying to do too much, trying to be too perfect,” Smith said. “That’s kind of what I ran into in the past.”</p><p>Venable turned to lefty Bryan Hudson, who retired DeLauter on a lineout to left. Then it was righty Jordan Hicks’ turn. He struck out Adell and Angel Martinez before walking pinch-hitter Nathaniel Lowe. In came lefty Anthony Kay, who allowed a double to Travis Bazzana and a walk to Austin Hedges. But he got Sox killer Brayan Rocchio to line out to right.</p><p>After Kay retired the side in order in the fifth, it was Taylor time.</p><p>“I was in the zone early,” Taylor said. “And even when I did fall behind, I was able to make good pitches to get right back into the count and get some soft contact.</p><p>Every game could be considered a bullpen game for the Sox, who used an opener 31 times in the regular season, more than any other MLB team. Sox relievers made 214 appearances with at least 1 ⅓ innings, breaking the major-league record set by the 2018 Rays (204). And the Sox’ bullpen led the majors with 766 innings, the third-highest total in major-league history.</p><p>But how long can the Sox get away with this? It worked in their two-game sweep of the Astros, which was followed by two days off. The Sox also have days off Sunday and Tuesday before back-to-back games Wednesday and Thursday (if necessary). So in the short term, they can use the schedule to their advantage and use pitchers longer more often.</p><p>If — by the grace of Pope Leo — they advance to the AL Championship Series, though, this won’t cut it. That series has a 2-3-2 format, and the Sox won’t have enough pieces to put together for three consecutive games.</p><p>But the Sox aren’t looking that far ahead. They only look at the next game on the schedule, and though Smith and Taylor, their most-used pitchers this postseason — won’t be available for it, they could come back for Game 3 at Rate Field and pitch another three or four innings.</p><p>The Sox don’t expect their method to become the newest trend in baseball. They do, though, like the trend it has created.</p><p>“I think for the most part, [pitching] will stay relatively normal to how it’s been,” Taylor said. “But I think it’s what’s worked for us, and we’re going to rely on it.”</p>

entries.title: Residents near Ryan Field welcome football back to the neighborhood — with apprehension about other events
entries.summary: <p>As the Northwestern University Wildcats took to the field in their highly anticipated new Evanston stadium Friday, nearby residents were mostly excited to welcome back the lively atmosphere that comes with a college football game.</p><p>But some aren't extending that same energy to concerts and other events the city wants to host there.</p><p>The new $875 million, 35,000-seat Ryan Field sits on the same site where the team played from its construction in 1926 until its demolition in early 2024. The area is heavily residential, with single-family homes surrounding the stadium. On game days, neighbors gather for barbecues and tailgates, and some of the players even live across the street. </p><p>Northwestern football and the fanfare that comes with it have become part of the neighborhood's culture and defined its vibe.</p><p>"We go to the games all the time, and our neighborhood always tailgates, and we have stuff going on," said Nicole Wroblewski, who has lived less than a block from Ryan Field for seven years. "Our neighborhood kind of rallies together, and it's pretty exciting."</p><h3>Ryan Field entertainment expansion worries some residents</h3><p>Residents say they're used to the hustle and bustle that accompanies living near a football stadium, but they didn't sign up to live near a concert venue. Evanston city officials want the ability to host concerts and other commercial events, which has some residents raising their eyebrows.</p><p>The nonprofit group the Most Livable City Association, along with residents, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2023/11/30/23982789/opponents-sue-city-evanston-approving-northwestern-ryan-field-stadium-concert-plans" target="_blank" >filed a lawsuit against the city</a> when plans were first announced in 2023, arguing the "commercialization" of the site would cause issues with noise, pollution and traffic. That lawsuit is still working its way through the appellate court system.</p><p>"When they're using it for their own activities, that's been going on for years, and that's fine," said Andrew Berman, retired Cook County judge and president of the Most Livable City Association. "But when they decide they're going to run it as a giant commercial venture, and escape paying property taxes like other commercial and residential properties pay, that's what we find really objectionable."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ca0000" name="image-ca0000"></a>
